Stratified Retention for Continual Adaptation Nishit Anand Ramani Duraiswami † Dinesh Manocha † Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park, USA Email: nishit@umd.edu Abstract Continual learning treats degradation on previously seen data as evidence of failure, a convention inherited from settings with a stationary prediction target, where a correct label remains correct indefinitely. World models do not satisfy this condition. Their prediction target is the environment, which changes, so knowledge that was accurate when acquired may later become false, and discarding it is required behavior rather than a defect. Non-stationary ground truth is well studied in the concept drift literature and in the temporal factuality of language models, but has not been formulated for world models, which are distinctive in that they also encode knowledge that must never be revised. We argue that continual world models require retention stratified by invariance timescale , separating invariants such as physics and object permanence, which must never be revised, from instance-level facts that should be revised as soon as the environment changes. Standard forgetting metrics cannot distinguish a world model that has correctly revised outdated knowledge from one that has suffered catastrophic forgetting, and consequently rank a frozen model highest, while existing physical-reasoning benchmarks evaluate only frozen checkpoints. We propose differential retention , which reports invariant regression testing across the adaptation stream jointly with revision latency, without aggregation. 2 2 footnotetext: Equal advising. 1 Introduction World models learn an executable approximation of environment dynamics, mapping a state and an action to a distribution over successor states, and are used to plan, to train policies in imagination, and to synthesize experience that would otherwise be costly or unsafe to collect. Recent systems have scaled this formulation considerably. Dreamer 4 trains agents entirely within a learned model of Minecraft from offline data alone [ 10 ] , while V-JEPA 2 pretrains on over one million hours of video and transfers to zero-shot robot manipulation by planning in a learned latent space [ 2 ] . Pretraining efficiency has improved in parallel, with LeVJEPA matching V-JEPA 2 at between 5.6 × 5.6\times and 20.8 × 20.8\times less total pretraining compute [ 14 ] . In each case the resulting model is trained once and deployed without further modification. The environments these models operate in do not stay fixed. A deployed system must detect when its predictions fail, absorb new evidence, and revise its account of the world. Continual learning supplies the tools for that revision, but rests on an assumption that world models do not satisfy: that the prediction target is stationary, so any decline in performance on previously learned material is a defect. That convention derives from supervised classification. An image of a cat continues to be an image of a cat, so a model that becomes less accurate on it has degraded. A world model instead approximates the dynamics and configuration of an environment, p ⁡ ( s t + 1 ∣ s t , a t ) p(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}) , the distribution over the next state s t + 1 s_{t+1} given the current state s t s_{t} and the action a t a_{t} taken at time t t . That environment is not fixed. When a road is reconstructed, an object is relocated, or a scene is rearranged, knowledge that was accurate at acquisition becomes false, and a model that continues to assert it is stale rather than faithful. This separates three phenomena that current practice reports as one. Catastrophic forgetting is the loss of knowledge that remains true, and is a defect. Deliberate unlearning is the removal of knowledge that remains true but is unwanted, and is well studied. Obsolescence is the retention of knowledge that has become false, where revision is mandatory. The concept drift literature is built on the premise that ground truth can change. Ashrafee et al. [1] observe that continual learning methods implicitly treat the data of earlier tasks as static. In language-model factuality, Jiang et al. [11] propose the Evaluation Misleading Rate, which counts how often a model gives an up-to-date answer and is marked wrong against an outdated benchmark label. The problem has not, however, been posed for world models, and does not carry over unchanged. In both settings above, nothing the model knows is permanently true, so any fact may be revised. A world model is different: the physical, geometric and causal structure it encodes should survive every update. World models are therefore the case where obsolescence coexists with hard invariants, and that combination changes what must be protected and what must be measured (Figure 1 ). (a) Protection should be monotone in τ \tau (b) What the pair of measurements separates Figure 1: (a) World-model knowledge stratified by invariance timescale τ \tau . Existing consolidation methods choose what to protect by importance to past performance, which is unrelated to τ \tau , whereas we argue protection (bar width) should increase with τ \tau . (b) Reporting invariant retention and revision latency jointly helps separate a model that has adapted correctly from one that is merely frozen. Standard forgetting metrics reward both high retention and slow revision, and are therefore maximized by the frozen model in the top-right quadrant. Contributions. We argue that obsolescence is a failure mode of continual world models distinct from catastrophic forgetting, and one that invariants make unavoidable (Sec. 2 ). We propose stratifying world-model knowledge by invariance timescale τ \tau , with protection increasing in τ \tau (Sec. 3 ). We then identify what current evaluation cannot measure (Sec. 4 ) and propose differential retention as a protocol that addresses it (Sec. 5 ). 2 World models break the stationary-target assumption A world model can be wrong about the past for two reasons, and its behavior alone will not tell you which. It never acquired the relevant knowledge, or it acquired that knowledge and the environment subsequently changed. Only the first constitutes a learning failure, yet the two are reported identically. The continual world-model literature has largely not been required to confront this, because its benchmarks are constructed such that the second case cannot arise. Kessler et al. [12] evaluate Continual-Dreamer on sequences of Minigrid and Minihack tasks, and Yang et al. [23] evaluate WMAR (World Models with Augmented Replay) on Procgen and Atari sequences. In both cases ground truth within a task is fixed throughout, so any subsequent degradation is genuinely forgetting. Sometimes the assumption is explicit. DRAGO [ 9 ] studies task sequences that share the same dynamics and differ only in reward. This is a reasonable simplification, but it is also exactly the setting in which knowledge can never go out of date. Where environments do change, world models accommodate the change poorly. Wan et al. [21] report that PlaNet and DreamerV2 adapt poorly to local changes in the environment. Nijjer [18] observes that in DreamerV3 with an unbounded replay buffer the world model retains essentially all measurable knowledge of earlier tasks while the policy degrades regardless, suggesting that where a world model fails to update, the mechanism need not be loss of stored information. The gap is therefore structural rather than accidental: the setting where obsolescence matters most is the one our benchmarks leave out. 3 Stratification by invariance timescale We propose organizing world-model knowledge not by task or by modality but by τ \tau , the timescale over which a given piece of knowledge remains true. τ \tau is a property of the environment, not of the model or its update schedule. Table 1: Strata of world-model knowledge ordered by invariance timescale τ \tau . Stratum τ \tau Examples Required behavior Invariants ∞ \infty gravity, object permanence, impenetrability, geometric consistency, action–effect structure never revised, as any change is a defect Environment regularities long room layout, road network, how other agents typically behave revised slowly, on accumulated evidence Instance configuration short where objects are, which door is open, current lighting revised promptly Transient state immediate who is moving where, momentary occlusion no retention expected Table 1 expresses a claim that is not reflected in current practice. Elastic weight consolidation [ 13 ] , replay [ 19 ] , and distillation-based consolidation [ 15 ] do decide what to protect, but they decide on the wrong basis: what was important for past performance, rather than how long that knowledge stays true. The two are unrelated. A parameter can be important for an earlier task while encoding a fact the environment has since invalidated, and these methods respond by protecting it most strongly. The result fails in both directions. Nothing in a standard continual pipeline checks that physical or geometric invariants survived an update, so the top stratum is under-protected. Meanwhile a replay buffer that faithfully stores the old layout of a room keeps reasserting it after the room has changed, so the lower strata are over-protected. Ashrafee et al. [1] fix the second problem in classification by evicting outdated exemplars. The world-model case also needs the first, which has no counterpart in their setting. LeJEPA [ 3 ] identifies the isotropic Gaussian as the embedding distribution that minimizes downstream prediction risk and enforces it with a regularizer that provably rules out representational collapse, an objective LeVJEPA extends to video [ 14 ] . No comparable proof exists that a representation will preserve a physical or geometric invariant once it starts updating. The available formal results describe what a representation must not do, but none describes what it must retain. This stratification is also distinct from multi-timescale memory. The Continuum Memory System of Behrouz et al. [4] , building on Titans [ 5 ] , stratifies memory modules by update frequency, whereas ours stratifies by the rate at which ground truth moves. Only the latter tells you whether a change was correct: a fast-updating module that revises a physical invariant is behaving exactly as designed, and is still wrong, because the invariant it revised did not change. The top stratum is not only physics. Object permanence, geometric consistency, causal action–effect structure, and the agent’s model of its own body are all knowledge that should not be altered. Physics is simply the part for which probes already exist. 4 What current evaluation cannot measure Standard continual-learning metrics such as backward transfer and the forgetting measure compute performance on an earlier task before and after subsequent learning and interpret any decrease as forgetting. They cannot see the distinction drawn in Sec. 2 . A model that degrades because it has broken and a model that degrades because it correctly revised knowledge the environment has since invalidated produce the same number. Díaz-Rodríguez et al. [7] argued that forgetting alone is insufficient for evaluating continual learners and proposed axes covering transfer, memory and efficiency. None of them asks whether a degradation was warranted. This creates a perverse optimum: the best possible forgetting score belongs to a model that never updates at all. In a stationary benchmark this is harmless, since such a model also performs poorly on subsequent tasks. In a changing environment it is not, because the frozen model is precisely the failure mode continual adaptation is intended to remedy. A second gap follows. In classification and textual factuality the metric can be repaired by refreshing the labels, but in world models this is insufficient, because matching a refreshed target says nothing about whether the invariants survived the update. A model that accommodates a rearranged scene by degrading its representation of object permanence would score well under any updated-target metric. 5 Differential Retention We propose evaluating a continual world model on two quantities, reported separately. (a) Invariant regression testing. We fix a probe set drawn from the τ = ∞ \tau=\infty stratum, held out from the adaptation data, and re-run it after every adaptation round. A single evaluation at the end cannot show which update damaged an invariant. Concept-isolated physical probes already exist and are directly reusable. WorldBench [ 20 ] disentangles individual physical concepts to support per-concept diagnosis, and PhyGround [ 16 ] covers thirteen physical laws spanning solid-body mechanics, fluid dynamics and optics. Both, as published, evaluate frozen models. Applying them as a regression suite across an adaptation stream is, to our knowledge, not done in the literature, and requires no new data, only a change in when the probes are run. (b) Revision latency. We measure how many observations the model needs before its predictions reflect a fact that has changed, and count separately the facts it never revises at all. Neither quantity is informative on its own, as Figure 1 (b) shows. A frozen model scores well on invariant retention and fails on revision latency, while a model that adapts by overwriting scores well on revision latency and fails on invariant retention. Only a model that satisfies both is doing what continual adaptation is meant to achieve, and no single number can capture that. Maes et al. [17] report that recoloring the background in Push-T reduces planning success from 50.8 % 50.8\% to 6.0 % 6.0\% for both LeWM and PLDM, and conclude that current world models remain brittle under distribution shift. Were such a model permitted to adapt online and observed to recover, current evaluation cannot determine whether recovery occurred through correct revision of an appearance prior or through degradation of the dynamics model into a form that happens to score well on the task at hand. We note that (a) is implementable today only for the physical sub-case, since comparable probes for geometric consistency and causal structure do not yet exist. 6 Related Work Continual world models. Kessler et al. [12] find that reservoir sampling over past experience robustly mitigates forgetting, and adopt it as the replay strategy of Continual-Dreamer. Yang et al. [23] make the buffer memory-efficient by matching the distribution of past experience, and Fu et al. [9] avoid storing data at all by rehearsing synthetic trajectories. All three assume a fixed target. Non-stationary ground truth. The concept drift literature supplies the framing we adopt [ 1 , 6 ] , and Jiang et al. [11] build the closest existing metric, though for language-model factuality. Evaluating world models. Upadhyay et al. [20] and Lin et al. [16] isolate individual physical concepts so that failures can be attributed to specific laws, Maes et al. [17] document how sharply performance falls outside the training distribution, and Xing et al. [22] argue more broadly about what a world model is for. Memory and plasticity. Behrouz et al. [4] , Behrouz et al. [5] stratify memory by update frequency, which we contrast with ours in Sec. 3 . Dohare et al. [8] show that networks lose the capacity to learn over long streams, a constraint on any continual scheme. 7 Limitations and open questions As a position paper, this work contributes a framing and an evaluation protocol rather than experimental results, and we identify three questions that the framing raises. First, the strata in Table 1 are a starting proposal, their boundaries are likely domain-dependent, and whether τ \tau can be estimated from observation or must be supplied as domain knowledge remains unclear. Second, probes of sufficient rigor exist today only for physical invariants, so realizing the protocol in full requires comparable probes for geometric consistency and causal structure. Finally, whether invariants are localized in a learned world model is not yet known, and if they are entangled with its other knowledge, stratified retention may need architectural support. It never acquired the relevant knowledge, or it acquired that knowledge and the environment subsequently changed. Only the first constitutes a learning failure, yet the two are reported identically. The continual world-model literature has largely not been required to confront this, because its benchmarks are constructed such that the second case cannot arise. Kessler et al. [12] evaluate Continual-Dreamer on sequences of Minigrid and Minihack tasks, and Yang et al. [23] evaluate WMAR (World Models with Augmented Replay) on Procgen and Atari sequences. In both cases ground truth within a task is fixed throughout, so any subsequent degradation is genuinely forgetting. Sometimes the assumption is explicit. DRAGO [ 9 ] studies task sequences that share the same dynamics and differ only in reward. This is a reasonable simplification, but it is also exactly the setting in which knowledge can never go out of date. Where environments do change, world models accommodate the change poorly. Wan et al. [21] report that PlaNet and DreamerV2 adapt poorly to local changes in the environment. Nijjer [18] observes that in DreamerV3 with an unbounded replay buffer the world model retains essentially all measurable knowledge of earlier tasks while the policy degrades regardless, suggesting that where a world model fails to update, the mechanism need not be loss of stored information. The gap is therefore structural rather than accidental: the setting where obsolescence matters most is the one our benchmarks leave out. 3 Stratification by invariance timescale We propose organizing world-model knowledge not by task or by modality but by τ \tau , the timescale over which a given piece of knowledge remains true. τ \tau is a property of the environment, not of the model or its update schedule. Table 1: Strata of world-model knowledge ordered by invariance timescale τ \tau . Stratum τ \tau Examples Required behavior Invariants ∞ \infty gravity, object permanence, impenetrability, geometric consistency, action–effect structure never revised, as any change is a defect Environment regularities long room layout, road network, how other agents typically behave revised slowly, on accumulated evidence Instance configuration short where objects are, which door is open, current lighting revised promptly Transient state immediate who is moving where, momentary occlusion no retention expected Table 1 expresses a claim that is not reflected in current practice. Elastic weight consolidation [ 13 ] , replay [ 19 ] , and distillation-based consolidation [ 15 ] do decide what to protect, but they decide on the wrong basis: what was important for past performance, rather than how long that knowledge stays true. The two are unrelated. A parameter can be important for an earlier task while encoding a fact the environment has since invalidated, and these methods respond by protecting it most strongly. The result fails in both directions. Nothing in a standard continual pipeline checks that physical or geometric invariants survived an update, so the top stratum is under-protected. Meanwhile a replay buffer that faithfully stores the old layout of a room keeps reasserting it after the room has changed, so the lower strata are over-protected. Ashrafee et al. [1] fix the second problem in classification by evicting outdated exemplars. The world-model case also needs the first, which has no counterpart in their setting. LeJEPA [ 3 ] identifies the isotropic Gaussian as the embedding distribution that minimizes downstream prediction risk and enforces it with a regularizer that provably rules out representational collapse, an objective LeVJEPA extends to video [ 14 ] . No comparable proof exists that a representation will preserve a physical or geometric invariant once it starts updating. The available formal results describe what a representation must not do, but none describes what it must retain. This stratification is also distinct from multi-timescale memory. The Continuum Memory System of Behrouz et al. [4] , building on Titans [ 5 ] , stratifies memory modules by update frequency, whereas ours stratifies by the rate at which ground truth moves. Only the latter tells you whether a change was correct: a fast-updating module that revises a physical invariant is behaving exactly as designed, and is still wrong, because the invariant it revised did not change. The top stratum is not only physics. Object permanence, geometric consistency, causal action–effect structure, and the agent’s model of its own body are all knowledge that should not be altered. Physics is simply the part for which probes already exist. 4 What current evaluation cannot measure Standard continual-learning metrics such as backward transfer and the forgetting measure compute performance on an earlier task before and after subsequent learning and interpret any decrease as forgetting. They cannot see the distinction drawn in Sec. 2 . A model that degrades because it has broken and a model that degrades because it correctly revised knowledge the environment has since invalidated produce the same number. Díaz-Rodríguez et al. [7] argued that forgetting alone is insufficient for evaluating continual learners and proposed axes covering transfer, memory and efficiency. None of them asks whether a degradation was warranted. This creates a perverse optimum: the best possible forgetting score belongs to a model that never updates at all. In a stationary benchmark this is harmless, since such a model also performs poorly on subsequent tasks. In a changing environment it is not, because the frozen model is precisely the failure mode continual adaptation is intended to remedy. A second gap follows. In classification and textual factuality the metric can be repaired by refreshing the labels, but in world models this is insufficient, because matching a refreshed target says nothing about whether the invariants survived the update. A model that accommodates a rearranged scene by degrading its representation of object permanence would score well under any updated-target metric. 5 Differential Retention We propose evaluating a continual world model on two quantities, reported separately. (a) Invariant regression testing. We fix a probe set drawn from the τ = ∞ \tau=\infty stratum, held out from the adaptation data, and re-run it after every adaptation round. A single evaluation at the end cannot show which update damaged an invariant. Concept-isolated physical probes already exist and are directly reusable. WorldBench [ 20 ] disentangles individual physical concepts to support per-concept diagnosis, and PhyGround [ 16 ] covers thirteen physical laws spanning solid-body mechanics, fluid dynamics and optics. Both, as published, evaluate frozen models. Applying them as a regression suite across an adaptation stream is, to our knowledge, not done in the literature, and requires no new data, only a change in when the probes are run. (b) Revision latency. We measure how many observations the model needs before its predictions reflect a fact that has changed, and count separately the facts it never revises at all. Neither quantity is informative on its own, as Figure 1 (b) shows. A frozen model scores well on invariant retention and fails on revision latency, while a model that adapts by overwriting scores well on revision latency and fails on invariant retention. Only a model that satisfies both is doing what continual adaptation is meant to achieve, and no single number can capture that. Maes et al. [17] report that recoloring the background in Push-T reduces planning success from 50.8 % 50.8\% to 6.0 % 6.0\% for both LeWM and PLDM, and conclude that current world models remain brittle under distribution shift. Were such a model permitted to adapt online and observed to recover, current evaluation cannot determine whether recovery occurred through correct revision of an appearance prior or through degradation of the dynamics model into a form that happens to score well on the task at hand. We note that (a) is implementable today only for the physical sub-case, since comparable probes for geometric consistency and causal structure do not yet exist. 6 Related Work Continual world models. Kessler et al. [12] find that reservoir sampling over past experience robustly mitigates forgetting, and adopt it as the replay strategy of Continual-Dreamer. Yang et al. [23] make the buffer memory-efficient by matching the distribution of past experience, and Fu et al. [9] avoid storing data at all by rehearsing synthetic trajectories. All three assume a fixed target. Non-stationary ground truth. The concept drift literature supplies the framing we adopt [ 1 , 6 ] , and Jiang et al. [11] build the closest existing metric, though for language-model factuality. Evaluating world models. Upadhyay et al. [20] and Lin et al. [16] isolate individual physical concepts so that failures can be attributed to specific laws, Maes et al. [17] document how sharply performance falls outside the training distribution, and Xing et al. [22] argue more broadly about what a world model is for. Memory and plasticity. Behrouz et al. [4] , Behrouz et al. [5] stratify memory by update frequency, which we contrast with ours in Sec. 3 . Dohare et al. [8] show that networks lose the capacity to learn over long streams, a constraint on any continual scheme. 7 Limitations and open questions As a position paper, this work contributes a framing and an evaluation protocol rather than experimental results, and we identify three questions that the framing raises. First, the strata in Table 1 are a starting proposal, their boundaries are likely domain-dependent, and whether τ \tau can be estimated from observation or must be supplied as domain knowledge remains unclear. Second, probes of sufficient rigor exist today only for physical invariants, so realizing the protocol in full requires comparable probes for geometric consistency and causal structure. Finally, whether invariants are localized in a learned world model is not yet known, and if they are entangled with its other knowledge, stratified retention may need architectural support. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.03712 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Oct 2026] Title: RNADyn: A Benchmark for Generating and Understanding RNA Dynamics Authors: Yiming Huang , Lennart Bastian , Hanqun Cao , Luis Vollmers , Tolga Birdal View a PDF of the paper titled RNADyn: A Benchmark for Generating and Understanding RNA Dynamics, by Yiming Huang and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) functions through conformational changes that are not fully captured by static structures. However, large-scale standardized RNA dynamics data remain limited, and existing approaches typically treat trajectory generation and dynamics understanding as separate objectives. Here, we introduce RNADynBench, a standardized RNA molecular dynamics (MD) benchmark with 2585 quality-controlled 100-ns all-atom trajectories and leakage-controlled splits. Building on RNADynBench, we develop RNADynNet, a unified model for RNA dynamics learning that uses a shared backbone for both trajectory generation and dynamics fingerprint extraction from a single conformer. It combines coordinate denoising, single-frame-to-trajectory alignment, and physical grounding to connect all-atom trajectory generation with dynamics representation learning. Physical grounding improves both generated dynamics and the physical information recoverable from these fingerprints. Across both test sets, including the high-flexibility challenge set, the generated trajectories achieve RMSF correlations of 0.875 and 0.766, while single-conformer predictions show comparable agreement with MD-derived dynamics. RNADynBench and RNADynNet together establish a benchmark and unified modeling framework for generating and understanding RNA dynamics. Data Curation RNADynBench is constructed from experimentally resolved RNA structures retrieved from RNA-Solo, a repository of cleaned PDB-derived RNA structures \citep RNASolo-2022. For each entry, we retrieve the original PDB/mmCIF records by PDB ID to recover its molecular context before curation. We retain the RNA-Solo target chain or chains. Additional RNA chains are retained only if their chain assignments are reliable, they contact the target within 5 Å (heavy atoms) after non-RNA components are removed, and they meet the partner-size limit. When partners are retained, the combined RNA length is limited to 512 nucleotides. Missing atoms and modified nucleotides are thus only handled when residue identity and topology remain unambiguous. LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients Lyuxin David Zhang Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Eric Wong Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Surbhi Goel Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Anton Xue Affiliation: University of Texas at Austin Abstract The choice of post-training data for large language models substantially affects downstream performance. Gradient-based data selection is a popular approach that ranks training data by how well their gradients align with those of a small validation set. However, ranking with full-parameter gradients requires an expensive backward pass on every sample, making computation intractable for large candidate pools. This raises a natural question: can we approximate full-gradient features at a fraction of the cost? Conveniently, we find that output-layer gradients suffice for effective data selection, yet require only the cheaper forward pass. We implement this as LESSER, a drop-in wrapper for selection methods that reduces the feature-extraction FLOP cost by 9.7 × 9.7	imes for SFT and 3.0 × 3.0	imes for RL benchmarks, while tracking full-gradient performance on downstream tasks. Empirically, we find that even when output-layer and full gradients rank individual samples differently, they select batches with aligned gradients. Figure 1: Efficient data selection with output-layer gradients. Given a candidate training pool and a small query set representative of downstream tasks, LESSER extracts output-layer gradient features to rank and select training examples. These features approximate the downstream behavior of full-gradient methods like LESS while substantially reducing feature-extraction FLOPs. 1 Introduction The choice of post-training data substantially shapes the performance of large language models (LLMs) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . In particular, training on small, high-quality subsets tailored to a target task can match or even outperform training on a larger, general pool ( Xia et al., 2024 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) . However, identifying which subset to use is non-trivial, as the utility of each sample depends on the model and target task, and selection can become expensive when the candidate pool grows. These challenges have motivated the development of data selection methods for identifying targeted, high-quality subsets ( Killamsetty et al., 2021b ) . A common approach to targeted data selection maps candidate and query examples into a shared feature space and selects candidates by their similarity to the queries ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . When choosing features, gradients are a natural choice because they describe how each training sample would update the model. This principle underlies modern LLM data selection methods such as LESS ( Xia et al., 2024 ) and GIST ( Min et al., 2026 ) for SFT, GradAlign ( Yang et al., 2026 ) for RL, and GRACE ( Panigrahi et al., 2025 ) for distillation teacher selection. However, full-parameter gradients are costly to compute at scale: each candidate requires a backward pass through the LLM. For large candidate pools, extraction can cost more than training on the selected data itself ( Yin and Rush, 2024 ) . This has motivated more compute-efficient features, such as RDS+ ( Ivison et al., 2025 ) , which uses hidden-state features, and proxy-model methods such as Yang et al. (2024b) , which use smaller models to guide selection. Despite their cost, however, gradient-based features often yield superior subsets ( Nayak et al., 2026 ) . We thus aim to approximate gradients at a fraction of the cost. In particular, output-layer gradients are attractive because they can be computed directly from last-layer hidden states and output probabilities available during a forward pass, without backpropagating through the model. These features have also proved useful in other settings, including active learning for vision models ( Ash et al., 2019 ) , data valuation ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , and data attribution ( Ran et al., 2026 ) methods. We find that they are also effective for post-training data selection. 1.1 Our contributions We propose LESSER ( L ast-layer E rror S ignals for S calable E xample R anking), a drop-in wrapper for gradient-based data selection methods that only swaps in output-layer gradients, leaving the selection rule unchanged. We implement this for LESS in SFT data selection, for GradAlign in RL problem selection, and for GRACE in distillation teacher selection. LESSER is cost-efficient. Extracting output-layer gradients is cost-efficient, requiring 9.7 × 9.7	imes fewer FLOPs on SFT and 3.0 × 3.0	imes fewer FLOPs on RL. This effect is more pronounced in our wall-clock experiments (Section 4 ), where LESSER reduces feature-extraction time by 17.8 × 17.8	imes in SFT, the added scoring time per selection round by 3.5 × 3.5	imes in RL, and feature-extraction time by 3.9 3.9 – 5.4 × 5.4	imes in distillation teacher selection. LESSER tracks full-gradient performance. Across a variety of setups, output-layer gradients find subsets that reach downstream performance similar to that of subsets found with full gradients. • SFT. Across five SFT tasks and four LLMs, the absolute downstream score gap between LESSER and LESS averages only 1.3 1.3 points, growing to 2.2 2.2 against RDS+ , and to 2.6 2.6 against a random selection baseline. Relative to LESS -selected batches, the centered gradient cosine similarity is 0.29 0.29 for LESSER , compared with 0.03 0.03 for RDS+ and approximately zero for Random. At the base model, the batch gradients of LESSER selections thus align with those of LESS more than other baselines do. • RL . In RL, the problems LESSER and GradAlign select in the first round have a Jaccard similarity of 0.53 0.53 , compared to the random baseline’s 0.075 0.075 . After training, LESSER and GradAlign reach the same final test accuracy. • Distillation. Across three different distillation settings, LESSER consistently selects the same top teacher from a pool of 10 10 to 14 14 teachers as the unmodified GRACE. This suggests that GRACE’s teacher choice is robust to replacing full gradients with output-layer gradients. 1.2 Related work Targeted data selection. Data selection methods differ in the notion of usefulness they aim to capture. Quality filtering and diversity-based curation seek examples that are broadly useful for instruction tuning ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Other methods select data relative to a reference distribution or dataset: DSIR ( Xie et al., 2023 ) matches a target text distribution for pretraining, while CRAIG ( Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020 ) constructs weighted subsets that approximate the full training-set gradient. Selection can also be tied directly to a training objective: GLISTER ( Killamsetty et al., 2021b ) optimizes held-out validation performance, while GRAD-MATCH ( Killamsetty et al., 2021a ) matches the gradient of the training or validation set. For targeted post-training, LESS ( Xia et al., 2024 ) uses gradient alignment and RDS+ ( Ivison et al., 2025 ) uses hidden-state similarity. GIST ( Min et al., 2026 ) projects gradients into a subspace defined by validation gradients, while GradAlign ( Yang et al., 2026 ) uses policy-gradient alignment for online RL selection. Systematic evaluations show that selection gains vary across datasets and budgets ( Diddee and Ippolito, 2025 ; Nayak et al., 2026 ) , and that the cost of selection can outweigh its training gains ( Yin and Rush, 2024 ) . We instead focus on the efficiency of data selection pipelines, and show that output-layer gradients are a cost-efficient substitute for full-gradient features. Efficient gradient representations. Gradient-based attribution connects training examples to their effects on model predictions. Gradient-based data selection is a popular approach that ranks training data by how well their gradients align with those of a small validation set. However, ranking with full-parameter gradients requires an expensive backward pass on every sample, making computation intractable for large candidate pools. This raises a natural question: can we approximate full-gradient features at a fraction of the cost? Conveniently, we find that output-layer gradients suffice for effective data selection, yet require only the cheaper forward pass. We implement this as LESSER, a drop-in wrapper for selection methods that reduces the feature-extraction FLOP cost by 9.7 × 9.7	imes for SFT and 3.0 × 3.0	imes for RL benchmarks, while tracking full-gradient performance on downstream tasks. Empirically, we find that even when output-layer and full gradients rank individual samples differently, they select batches with aligned gradients. Figure 1: Efficient data selection with output-layer gradients. Given a candidate training pool and a small query set representative of downstream tasks, LESSER extracts output-layer gradient features to rank and select training examples. These features approximate the downstream behavior of full-gradient methods like LESS while substantially reducing feature-extraction FLOPs. 1 Introduction The choice of post-training data substantially shapes the performance of large language models (LLMs) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . In particular, training on small, high-quality subsets tailored to a target task can match or even outperform training on a larger, general pool ( Xia et al., 2024 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) . However, identifying which subset to use is non-trivial, as the utility of each sample depends on the model and target task, and selection can become expensive when the candidate pool grows. These challenges have motivated the development of data selection methods for identifying targeted, high-quality subsets ( Killamsetty et al., 2021b ) . A common approach to targeted data selection maps candidate and query examples into a shared feature space and selects candidates by their similarity to the queries ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . When choosing features, gradients are a natural choice because they describe how each training sample would update the model. This principle underlies modern LLM data selection methods such as LESS ( Xia et al., 2024 ) and GIST ( Min et al., 2026 ) for SFT, GradAlign ( Yang et al., 2026 ) for RL, and GRACE ( Panigrahi et al., 2025 ) for distillation teacher selection. However, full-parameter gradients are costly to compute at scale: each candidate requires a backward pass through the LLM. For large candidate pools, extraction can cost more than training on the selected data itself ( Yin and Rush, 2024 ) . This has motivated more compute-efficient features, such as RDS+ ( Ivison et al., 2025 ) , which uses hidden-state features, and proxy-model methods such as Yang et al. (2024b) , which use smaller models to guide selection. Despite their cost, however, gradient-based features often yield superior subsets ( Nayak et al., 2026 ) . We thus aim to approximate gradients at a fraction of the cost. In particular, output-layer gradients are attractive because they can be computed directly from last-layer hidden states and output probabilities available during a forward pass, without backpropagating through the model. These features have also proved useful in other settings, including active learning for vision models ( Ash et al., 2019 ) , data valuation ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , and data attribution ( Ran et al., 2026 ) methods. We find that they are also effective for post-training data selection. 1.1 Our contributions We propose LESSER ( L ast-layer E rror S ignals for S calable E xample R anking), a drop-in wrapper for gradient-based data selection methods that only swaps in output-layer gradients, leaving the selection rule unchanged. We implement this for LESS in SFT data selection, for GradAlign in RL problem selection, and for GRACE in distillation teacher selection. LESSER is cost-efficient. Extracting output-layer gradients is cost-efficient, requiring 9.7 × 9.7	imes fewer FLOPs on SFT and 3.0 × 3.0	imes fewer FLOPs on RL. This effect is more pronounced in our wall-clock experiments (Section 4 ), where LESSER reduces feature-extraction time by 17.8 × 17.8	imes in SFT, the added scoring time per selection round by 3.5 × 3.5	imes in RL, and feature-extraction time by 3.9 3.9 – 5.4 × 5.4	imes in distillation teacher selection. LESSER tracks full-gradient performance. Across a variety of setups, output-layer gradients find subsets that reach downstream performance similar to that of subsets found with full gradients. • SFT. Across five SFT tasks and four LLMs, the absolute downstream score gap between LESSER and LESS averages only 1.3 1.3 points, growing to 2.2 2.2 against RDS+ , and to 2.6 2.6 against a random selection baseline. Relative to LESS -selected batches, the centered gradient cosine similarity is 0.29 0.29 for LESSER , compared with 0.03 0.03 for RDS+ and approximately zero for Random. At the base model, the batch gradients of LESSER selections thus align with those of LESS more than other baselines do. • RL . In RL, the problems LESSER and GradAlign select in the first round have a Jaccard similarity of 0.53 0.53 , compared to the random baseline’s 0.075 0.075 . After training, LESSER and GradAlign reach the same final test accuracy. • Distillation. Across three different distillation settings, LESSER consistently selects the same top teacher from a pool of 10 10 to 14 14 teachers as the unmodified GRACE. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.03679 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Oct 2026] Title: Simulation-Free Learning of Population Dynamics with Wasserstein Lagrangian Residuals Authors: Fedor Sergeev , Markus Heinonen , Daniel Waxman , Tim Cooijmans , Ricardo Baptista , Dmitry Batenkov , Eli Bingham View a PDF of the paper titled Simulation-Free Learning of Population Dynamics with Wasserstein Lagrangian Residuals, by Fedor Sergeev and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The dynamics of cells, organisms, and fluids are often modeled as probability distributions evolving over time. Reconstructing and extrapolating this evolution from unpaired snapshots requires assumptions about the underlying process. Wasserstein gradient flows are a common choice, but they cannot describe conservative or periodic dynamics. Lagrangian mechanics in Wasserstein space covers both, but existing methods for learning it are simulation-based: they run a numerical solver at every training step, which makes training expensive. We propose Double-Stitch, a simulation-free method that learns these mechanics by penalizing the residual of the equation of motion along a learned population path. We derive this equation from a Clebsch variational principle that does not require gradient velocities, and show that the residual vanishes exactly when the equation holds. We test Double-Stitch on synthetic, single-cell and ocean vortex datasets and find that it matches or outperforms gradient-flow methods and simulation-based WLM on most tasks, while training $4$-$14$ times faster than WLM. We provide a JAX implementation of Double-Stitch at this https URL . Simulation-Free Learning of Population Dynamics with Wasserstein Lagrangian Residuals Fedor Sergeev † † thanks: Correspondence to fedor.sergeev@inf.ethz.ch Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Helmholtz AI Markus Heinonen Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Daniel Waxman Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: MIT Tim Cooijmans Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Ricardo Baptista Dmitry Batenkov Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: University of Toronto Eli Bingham Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Abstract The dynamics of cells, organisms, and fluids are often modeled as probability distributions evolving over time. Reconstructing and extrapolating this evolution from unpaired snapshots requires assumptions about the underlying process. Wasserstein gradient flows are a common choice, but they cannot describe conservative or periodic dynamics. Lagrangian mechanics in Wasserstein space covers both, but existing methods for learning it are simulation-based: they run a numerical solver at every training step, which makes training expensive. We propose Double-Stitch , a simulation-free method that learns these mechanics by penalizing the residual of the equation of motion along a learned population path. We derive this equation from a Clebsch variational principle that does not require gradient velocities, and show that the residual vanishes exactly when the equation holds. We test Double-Stitch on synthetic, single-cell and ocean vortex datasets and find that it matches or outperforms gradient-flow methods and simulation-based WLM on most tasks, while training 4 4 – 14 14 times faster than WLM. We provide a JAX implementation of Double-Stitch at https://github.com/BasisResearch/stitching . 1 Introduction Learning complex dynamics of populations is a fundamental problem with applications to single-cell biology, animal behavior, and fluid mechanics ( Schiebinger et al., 2019 ; Maury et al., 2010 ; Petrović et al., 2025 ) . Individual entities are usually not tracked: the population is observed as unpaired sets of samples (snapshots) measured at several time points. Generally, modeling approaches to this problem can be grouped into three families based on the assumptions they make about the data generating process: flow-based, gradient flow, and Lagrangian flow. Flow-based methods do not make explicit assumptions 1 1 1 Some methods can use a reference process, but it is designed for a specific dataset, not used as a general assumption ( Petrović et al., 2025 ) . about the underlying dynamical process ( Kapuśniak et al., 2024 ; Atanackovic et al., 2025 ) . They learn a time-dependent velocity field or a stochastic bridge that transports an observed snapshot to a new time point by an optimal path (e.g., minimizing a kinetic energy). Without additional assumptions, these methods are generally not suited for extrapolation beyond the observed time interval ( Guan et al., 2026a ) . Gradient flow methods assume that the underlying dynamics follow the steepest descent of a free energy in Wasserstein space, or, in other words, a Wasserstein gradient flow (WGF). The resulting closed system allows learning the time-independent free energy function ℱ \mathcal{F} and therefore provides time extrapolation capabilities. However, WGFs are purely dissipative and cannot effectively model dynamics where velocity is not deterministically defined by energy alone (e.g., as in periodic phenomena and conservative systems; see the conservative example in Figure 1 ). The Lagrangian methods generalize gradient flows by assuming that the underlying dynamic process is governed by an equation on acceleration instead of velocity (i.e., Newton’s second law). This approach was recently proposed for population dynamics ( Guan et al., 2026a ) , building on Lagrangian formulations in Wasserstein space ( Neklyudov et al., 2024 ) . However, the existing algorithm (WLM) is simulation-based and computationally expensive because it simulates the trajectory at every training step. We propose Double-Stitch , a simulation-free approach to learning Lagrangian mechanics. Unlike flow-based methods, this method allows extrapolation; unlike WGF-based methods, it models periodic and conservative systems (see Figure 1 ); and it is computationally cheaper than the simulation-based WLM algorithm. Table 1 summarizes the similarities and differences between the existing methods and our approach. Double-Stitch is based on Stitching ( Heinonen et al., 2026 ) , a simulation-free WGF-based algorithm that learns the dynamics by directly optimizing the trajectory to minimize (a) the distance between the learned and observed snapshots, and (b) the residual of the underlying dynamical law. Double in the name refers to the second-order law, compared to the first-order equation for WGF. We re-derive the Wasserstein Lagrangian law without requiring gradient velocities and show its residual vanishes if and only if the dynamics are satisfied. Figure 1: Simulation-free fitting across three dynamical regimes. Left: conservative, damped and gradient-flow examples, with analytic densities, energies and Double-Stitch fits. Right: schematic training procedures for Double-Stitch and WLM. Grey curves show kinetic and total energy for the oscillators; the gradient-flow panel shows free energy. Grey contours show analytic densities. Contributions • We propose a Clebsch-based derivation of the Wasserstein Lagrangian mechanics. This derivation does not restrict the velocities to be gradient, making it applicable to initial conditions with rotational components. • We propose Double-Stitch, a simulation-free method that fits a latent population path and a neural potential by penalizing the discretized residual of the Lagrangian mechanics. • We show that Double-Stitch matches or improves upon competing methods for most tasks on synthetic, single-cell, and ocean vortex datasets, while being cheaper to train than WLM. Table 1: Comparison of methods for learning population dynamics. Double-Stitch is a simulation-free method that extrapolates in time and learns both gradient and second-order Lagrangian flows. Simulation-Free Learning of Population Dynamics with Wasserstein Lagrangian Residuals Fedor Sergeev † † thanks: Correspondence to fedor.sergeev@inf.ethz.ch Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Helmholtz AI Markus Heinonen Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Daniel Waxman Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: MIT Tim Cooijmans Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Ricardo Baptista Dmitry Batenkov Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Affiliation: University of Toronto Eli Bingham Affiliation: Basis Research Institute Abstract The dynamics of cells, organisms, and fluids are often modeled as probability distributions evolving over time. Reconstructing and extrapolating this evolution from unpaired snapshots requires assumptions about the underlying process. Wasserstein gradient flows are a common choice, but they cannot describe conservative or periodic dynamics. Lagrangian mechanics in Wasserstein space covers both, but existing methods for learning it are simulation-based: they run a numerical solver at every training step, which makes training expensive. We propose Double-Stitch , a simulation-free method that learns these mechanics by penalizing the residual of the equation of motion along a learned population path. We derive this equation from a Clebsch variational principle that does not require gradient velocities, and show that the residual vanishes exactly when the equation holds. We test Double-Stitch on synthetic, single-cell and ocean vortex datasets and find that it matches or outperforms gradient-flow methods and simulation-based WLM on most tasks, while training 4 4 – 14 14 times faster than WLM. We provide a JAX implementation of Double-Stitch at https://github.com/BasisResearch/stitching . 1 Introduction Learning complex dynamics of populations is a fundamental problem with applications to single-cell biology, animal behavior, and fluid mechanics ( Schiebinger et al., 2019 ; Maury et al., 2010 ; Petrović et al., 2025 ) . Individual entities are usually not tracked: the population is observed as unpaired sets of samples (snapshots) measured at several time points. Generally, modeling approaches to this problem can be grouped into three families based on the assumptions they make about the data generating process: flow-based, gradient flow, and Lagrangian flow. Flow-based methods do not make explicit assumptions 1 1 1 Some methods can use a reference process, but it is designed for a specific dataset, not used as a general assumption ( Petrović et al., 2025 ) . about the underlying dynamical process ( Kapuśniak et al., 2024 ; Atanackovic et al., 2025 ) . They learn a time-dependent velocity field or a stochastic bridge that transports an observed snapshot to a new time point by an optimal path (e.g., minimizing a kinetic energy). Without additional assumptions, these methods are generally not suited for extrapolation beyond the observed time interval ( Guan et al., 2026a ) . Gradient flow methods assume that the underlying dynamics follow the steepest descent of a free energy in Wasserstein space, or, in other words, a Wasserstein gradient flow (WGF). The resulting closed system allows learning the time-independent free energy function ℱ \mathcal{F} and therefore provides time extrapolation capabilities. However, WGFs are purely dissipative and cannot effectively model dynamics where velocity is not deterministically defined by energy alone (e.g., as in periodic phenomena and conservative systems; see the conservative example in Figure 1 ). The Lagrangian methods generalize gradient flows by assuming that the underlying dynamic process is governed by an equation on acceleration instead of velocity (i.e., Newton’s second law). This approach was recently proposed for population dynamics ( Guan et al., 2026a ) , building on Lagrangian formulations in Wasserstein space ( Neklyudov et al., 2024 ) . However, the existing algorithm (WLM) is simulation-based and computationally expensive because it simulates the trajectory at every training step. We propose Double-Stitch , a simulation-free approach to learning Lagrangian mechanics. Unlike flow-based methods, this method allows extrapolation; unlike WGF-based methods, it models periodic and conservative systems (see Figure 1 ); and it is computationally cheaper than the simulation-based WLM algorithm. Table 1 summarizes the similarities and differences between the existing methods and our approach. Double-Stitch is based on Stitching ( Heinonen et al., 2026 ) , a simulation-free WGF-based algorithm that learns the dynamics by directly optimizing the trajectory to minimize (a) the distance between the learned and observed snapshots, and (b) the residual of the underlying dynamical law. Double in the name refers to the second-order law, compared to the first-order equation for WGF. We re-derive the Wasserstein Lagrangian law without requiring gradient velocities and show its residual vanishes if and only if the dynamics are satisfied. Figure 1: Simulation-free fitting across three dynamical regimes. Left: conservative, damped and gradient-flow examples, with analytic densities, energies and Double-Stitch fits. Right: schematic training procedures for Double-Stitch and WLM. Grey curves show kinetic and total energy for the oscillators; the gradient-flow panel shows free energy. Grey contours show analytic densities. Contributions • We propose a Clebsch-based derivation of the Wasserstein Lagrangian mechanics. This derivation does not restrict the velocities to be gradient, making it applicable to initial conditions with rotational components. • We propose Double-Stitch, a simulation-free method that fits a latent population path and a neural potential by penalizing the discretized residual of the Lagrangian mechanics. • We show that Double-Stitch matches or improves upon competing methods for most tasks on synthetic, single-cell, and ocean vortex datasets, while being cheaper to train than WLM. Zeng , Bartosz Machura , Chuwen Liu , Paolo Tarantino , Coral Omene , Francisco J. Esteva , Rohit Bhargava , Marcin Braun , Kamila Paździerz , Jakub Czerwiński , Hanna Romańska-Knight , Albert Grinshpun , Bareket Daniel , Michele Buchinger , Frederick Howard , Piotr Wysocki , Brie Chun , Freya Schnabel , Rich Caruana , Jan Witowski , Krzysztof J. Geras View a PDF of the paper titled Transcriptome-informed multi-modal AI for predicting neoadjuvant therapy response from breast cancer biopsies, by Jungkyu Park and 24 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Scarcity of labeled data limits development of deep learning biomarkers in oncology. We develop a two-stage AI model predicting pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer. The first stage learns the transcriptome from histopathology using 8,742 patients across 32 cancer types, corroborated by pathologist review and spatial agreement with measured expression. This simplifies the second stage to predicting pCR from inferred expression and clinical variables. Developed using 1,080 patients (five cohorts) and evaluated in 1,412 patients (nine cohorts), the model achieves a pooled AUROC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.73-0.85), discriminating responders within molecular subtypes. It outperforms histopathological biomarkers, remaining stable across intratumoral sampling and with minimal biopsy tissue. Ablations show transcriptome-wide inference improves discrimination over clinical variables alone or one-stage pathology models, and robustness by avoiding genomic assays' gene selection constraints. These results indicate that biologically informed compression may generalize to data-sparse applications in precision oncology. Geras <krzysztof.geras@ataraxis.ai> . Abstract Scarcity of labeled data limits development of deep learning biomarkers in oncology. We develop a two-stage AI model predicting pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer. The first stage learns the transcriptome from histopathology using 8,742 patients across 32 cancer types, corroborated by pathologist review and spatial agreement with measured expression. This simplifies the second stage to predicting pCR from inferred expression and clinical variables. Developed using 1,080 patients (five cohorts) and evaluated in 1,412 patients (nine cohorts), the model achieves a pooled AUROC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.73–0.85), discriminating responders within molecular subtypes. It outperforms histopathological biomarkers, remaining stable across intratumoral sampling and with minimal biopsy tissue. Ablations show transcriptome-wide inference improves discrimination over clinical variables alone or one-stage pathology models, and robustness by avoiding genomic assays’ gene selection constraints. These results indicate that biologically informed compression may generalize to data-sparse applications in precision oncology. 1 Introduction Neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) is becoming the standard of care for early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)–positive patients, and is an established treatment option for selected patients with hormone receptor (HR)–positive/HER2-negative disease [ 59 , 67 ] . NAT allows response to be assessed at surgery, informs post-neoadjuvant treatment, and facilitates de-escalation of breast and axillary surgery [ 102 , 59 ] as well as adjuvant radiation therapy [ 70 ] . In addition, response-adapted de-escalation of chemotherapy [ 81 , 31 ] and omission of breast surgery in exceptional responders [ 61 ] are being investigated. Advances in neoadjuvant therapy have substantially improved pathological complete response (pCR) rates, with recent trials reporting improvements from 51.2% to 64.8% in early TNBC and from 56.3% to 67.3% in high-risk HER2 + + disease [ 92 , 45 ] . Despite these advances, approximately one third of patients still do not achieve pCR. For these patients, NAT entails months of systemic therapy, including cytotoxic chemotherapy [ 59 ] , and delayed definitive surgery, with the possibility of disease progression during treatment. In HR + + /HER2 − - disease, pCR is less common and its implications for long-term outcomes are less firmly established [ 97 ] . This highlights the need to identify, before treatment, patients at high risk of residual disease. However, accurate prediction at the patient level faces several challenges. First, the available data are limited: many existing datasets are small [ 90 , 2 , 50 , 32 , 75 ] , which has prevented models from reaching the robustness and accuracy required for routine clinical use. Second, existing biomarkers may lack sufficient expressivity to capture the biology that determines NAT response. These include genomic assays (e.g., HER2DX [ 86 ] ), receptor status (estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), HER2) [ 59 ] , and histological features such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) [ 26 , 25 , 44 , 57 , 71 , 98 , 69 ] . Within HR + + /HER2 − - patients, pCR rates vary with gene-expression scores [ 37 ] , motivating richer characterization of response-relevant biology beyond receptor status alone. Transcriptome-wide analyses indicate that molecular read-outs of the tumor phenotype may be informative for predicting NAT response [ 14 , 38 ] , but such research-grade assays are not clinically deployable at scale, and clinical RNA-based tests measure only small lists of targets (typically <100 genes [ 86 ] ). Histological features fare no better: TILs track response across subtypes but stratify coarsely [ 26 , 25 , 44 , 57 , 71 , 98 , 69 ] . Third, assessments themselves can be unstable, for two reasons: tumor sampling bias and observer variability. Needle biopsies typically sample less than one percent of the tumor bulk [ 64 ] . As breast tumors are heterogeneous ecosystems of malignant cells and their microenvironment [ 72 ] , this gives rise to tumor sampling bias [ 11 ] . When the genes of five gene expression assays were measured across matched regions of the same tumor, a quarter of patients crossed a risk-category boundary depending on which region was assayed [ 43 ] . Additionally, manual assessments add observer variability: scoring of TILs and Ki-67 is only moderately reproducible between observers and laboratories [ 60 , 85 ] . Stability to sampling is a prerequisite for a biopsy-based biomarker, yet it is seldom reported. Deep learning applied to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images offers a route to prediction that requires no additional tissue, molecular assay, or manual read. Foundation models—neural networks pretrained by self-supervised learning on millions of unlabeled tissue images [ 15 , 10 , 19 , 110 , 107 ] —convert any H&E slide into rich morphological representations (embeddings) without large annotated datasets. Turning those representations into a predictor of a clinical endpoint, however, still requires many labeled patients, and NAT cohorts with recorded response are small. Due to the large quantity and high dimensionality of pathology embeddings and the small NAT cohorts, we reasoned that dividing this learning problem into two stages could help: relating morphology to tumor biology, then relating that biology to treatment response. Existing pan-cancer cohorts pair each patient’s slides with a measured transcriptome—thousands of quantitative measurements per patient rather than one binary label. These paired data can teach a model how morphology relates to molecular features. Gene expression is also a useful intermediate representation because it both shapes treatment response and leaves visible traces in tissue morphology [ 91 , 48 , 83 ] . Learning to infer expression from these larger cohorts could leave the smaller NAT cohorts with the simpler task of relating inferred molecular features to response. Therefore, we built an AI model to infer gene expression from morphology and another AI model to predict pCR from the inferred expression [ 48 , 14 ] , rather than a single model to predict response directly from the slide. This design draws on broad transcriptional information without requiring an additional molecular assay or relying on a narrowly selected gene list, and yields an interpretable representation that can be related to NAT response biology. Here we present Ataraxis Breast NEO (hereafter NEO), a multi-modal AI model that estimates the probability of pCR from a pre-treatment biopsy H&E slide together with baseline clinical variables ( Figure 1 a). Its first step, MORPHEUS (Morphological Oncology Representation and Prediction of High-dimensional Expression Using Slides), is a pan-cancer model developed on 8,742 patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) [ 47 ] spanning 32 projects to infer the expression of 14,773 genes from morphology alone. Its second step predicts pCR from that inferred expression with the standard clinical variables. NEO was developed on 1,080 patients from five cohorts and evaluated on 1,412 patients from nine independent cohorts. We assessed four aspects: discrimination relative to benchmarks, added value beyond the clinical variables, explainability of the predictions, and stability to biopsy sampling. Figure 1: Overview of the study and NEO architecture. a , Clinical setting and prediction task. The tumor’s gene expression reflects its biological state, and that state also manifests in tissue morphology. The patient’s tumor is sampled by core needle biopsy and digitized as an H&E-stained whole-slide image (WSI). From this biopsy WSI, it is possible to infer gene expression, as a substrate for predicting the probability of pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant therapy (NAT). b , Development and evaluation cohorts. Left, the contributing institutions, with marker area proportional to cohort size. Right, two bar charts: cohort size and molecular subtype composition. In the size chart, bar length is the number of patients and the solid segment is those achieving pCR. Throughout, blue denotes the development set (5 cohorts, N = 1,080) and red denotes the held-out evaluation set (9 cohorts, N = 1,412). “Unknown” subtype covers patients whose HER2 status is equivocal or whose receptor status is not recorded. c , Distribution of the number of 224 × \times 224-pixel patches per slide across all 3,606 slides in both splits (log scale; median 4,123 per slide). d , Cohorts used to build and evaluate MORPHEUS. TCGA supplied the paired H&E slides and bulk RNA-seq on which MORPHEUS was developed; CPTAC was held out and used only for evaluation. Counts are patients, whole-slide images and distinct cancer types. e , MORPHEUS training and inference. Trained on TCGA cases with paired H&E slides and bulk RNA-seq, MORPHEUS infers expression from WSIs alone, requiring no transcriptomic assay at inference. f , NEO inference pipeline. MORPHEUS converts the biopsy WSI into H&E-inferred expression, which is combined with baseline clinical variables and mapped to a calibrated probability of pCR ( Section 4.2 ). 2 Results 2.1 Multi-national development and evaluation datasets We assembled a multi-national dataset of digitized H&E biopsy whole-slide images (WSIs) and clinical data from 14 breast cancer cohorts spanning seven countries across North America, Latin America, Europe, and the Middle East ( Figure 1 b). Five cohorts from three countries (Gundersen, Omica, TransNEO [ 90 ] , Yale [ 33 ] and NYU; N = 1,080) were used for development and nine independent cohorts from five countries (Protege, UChicago [ 49 ] , Nexus [ 103 ] , Dordrecht, IMPRESS [ 50 ] , Jagiellonian, Shaare Zedek, Providence [ 8 ] , and Łódź; N = 1,412) for evaluation, spanning diverse molecular subtypes and geographies. Of the development cohorts, Omica, Gundersen, and NYU were used for cross-validation (hereafter cross-validation cohorts), and TransNEO and Yale for training only ( Section 4.7 ). Cohort characteristics are given in Table 1 . The evaluation set ( Table 2 ), used for all reported pCR performance estimates, had an overall pCR rate of 37.3% and a near-even split across the molecular subtypes (36.7% TNBC, 31.5% HR + + /HER2 − - , 30.8% HER2 + + ). The label used for model development and evaluation was pCR, assessed at surgery as the absence of residual invasive disease in both the breast and regional lymph nodes, consistent with the NeoSTEEP definition [ 65 ] ( Section 4.1 ). Where available, response was additionally characterized by residual cancer burden (RCB) class [ 101 ] , from RCB-0 (equivalent to pCR) to RCB-III (extensive residual disease), which we used only as an exploratory secondary endpoint. As the evaluation cohorts differ in size, subtype composition, and pCR rate ( Figure 1 b), performance is pooled with a random-effects model throughout ( Section 4.9 ). This heterogeneity reflects real population differences, enabling a stronger assessment of generalizability. In total, the imaging data comprise 3,606 pre-treatment biopsy slides carrying 19.6 million 224 × \times 224-pixel tissue patches (median 4,123 per slide; Figure 1 c). The overall sample size of our study substantially exceeds that of most previously reported histopathology-based NAT response prediction studies [ 90 , 2 , 50 , 32 , 75 ] . 2.2 NEO: a multi-modal AI model for predicting neoadjuvant therapy response We developed NEO ( Figures 1 and 4.2 ), a multi-modal AI model that integrates routine pre-treatment biopsy H&E WSIs and baseline clinical variables to estimate the probability of achieving pCR. The model operates in two steps. First, MORPHEUS infers expression values for 14,773 protein-coding genes from the WSIs, referred to here as H&E-inferred expression ( Figure 1 e). Falcon [ 10 ] , a pathology foundation model trained by self-supervised learning, extracts a morphological embedding for every 224 × \times 224-pixel patch. A model trained on paired H&E and bulk RNA sequencing data from TCGA then aggregates these embeddings over the slide by multiple-instance learning (MIL) into expression values. Second, the H&E-inferred expression is compressed to five components ( Section 4.6 ) and combined with baseline clinical variables ( Section 4.1 ) to produce a calibrated probability of pCR ( Figure 1 f). This is the only step trained on response data: explainable boosting machines (EBMs) [ 74 , 16 ] and tabular ResNets [ 42 ] were fitted on the 1,080 development patients, calibrated post hoc ( Section A.2.11 ), and ensembled ( Section 4.8 ). 2.3 External evaluation and benchmarking of NEO We evaluated NEO on nine independent external cohorts comprising 1,412 patients ( Figure 2 ). NEO achieved a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.792 (95% CI, 0.732–0.852; p = 3.4 × 10 − 6 p=3.4\times 10^{-6} versus a null AUROC of 0.5), with substantial heterogeneity across cohorts ( I 2 I^{2} = 74%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0.0040; both defined in Section A.3 ). Discrimination was above chance in every cohort: per-cohort AUROCs ranged from 0.658 to 0.880, and all 95% confidence intervals excluded 0.5 ( Figure 1 ). Discrimination held within each molecular subtype ( Figure 2 a): 0.699 (95% CI, 0.643–0.755; I 2 I^{2} = 0%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0; seven cohorts) for TNBC, 0.669 (0.576–0.763; I 2 I^{2} = 58%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0.0077; eight cohorts) for HER2 + + , and 0.762 (0.686–0.837; I 2 I^{2} = 0%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0; six cohorts) for HR + + /HER2 − - disease, each pooled over the cohorts with sufficient samples of that subtype ( Section 4.9 ; per-cohort estimates in Figure 1 b–d). We next assessed calibration, the agreement between predicted and observed pCR rates ( Figure 2 b, Section 4.10 ). The calibration slope did not differ significantly from 1 in any stratum (all patients: 1.11, 95% CI, 0.97–1.25; TNBC: 1.21, 95% CI, 0.89–1.52; HER2 + + : 0.75, 95% CI, 0.47–1.04; HR + + /HER2 − - : 1.17, 95% CI, 0.84–1.51), consistent with appropriately dispersed predictions. The intercept indicated under-prediction overall (0.18, 95% CI, 0.06–0.30) and in HER2 + + disease (0.36, 95% CI, 0.16–0.56) and did not differ significantly from zero in TNBC (0.13, 95% CI, -0.05–0.32) and HR + + /HER2 − - disease (-0.06, 95% CI, -0.35–0.23).
