Geras <krzysztof.geras@ataraxis.ai> . Abstract Scarcity of labeled data limits development of deep learning biomarkers in oncology. We develop a two-stage AI model predicting pathological complete response (pCR) to neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer. The first stage learns the transcriptome from histopathology using 8,742 patients across 32 cancer types, corroborated by pathologist review and spatial agreement with measured expression. This simplifies the second stage to predicting pCR from inferred expression and clinical variables. Developed using 1,080 patients (five cohorts) and evaluated in 1,412 patients (nine cohorts), the model achieves a pooled AUROC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.73–0.85), discriminating responders within molecular subtypes. It outperforms histopathological biomarkers, remaining stable across intratumoral sampling and with minimal biopsy tissue. Ablations show transcriptome-wide inference improves discrimination over clinical variables alone or one-stage pathology models, and robustness by avoiding genomic assays’ gene selection constraints. These results indicate that biologically informed compression may generalize to data-sparse applications in precision oncology. 1 Introduction Neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) is becoming the standard of care for early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)–positive patients, and is an established treatment option for selected patients with hormone receptor (HR)–positive/HER2-negative disease [ 59 , 67 ] . NAT allows response to be assessed at surgery, informs post-neoadjuvant treatment, and facilitates de-escalation of breast and axillary surgery [ 102 , 59 ] as well as adjuvant radiation therapy [ 70 ] . In addition, response-adapted de-escalation of chemotherapy [ 81 , 31 ] and omission of breast surgery in exceptional responders [ 61 ] are being investigated. Advances in neoadjuvant therapy have substantially improved pathological complete response (pCR) rates, with recent trials reporting improvements from 51.2% to 64.8% in early TNBC and from 56.3% to 67.3% in high-risk HER2 + + disease [ 92 , 45 ] . Despite these advances, approximately one third of patients still do not achieve pCR. For these patients, NAT entails months of systemic therapy, including cytotoxic chemotherapy [ 59 ] , and delayed definitive surgery, with the possibility of disease progression during treatment. In HR + + /HER2 − - disease, pCR is less common and its implications for long-term outcomes are less firmly established [ 97 ] . This highlights the need to identify, before treatment, patients at high risk of residual disease. However, accurate prediction at the patient level faces several challenges. First, the available data are limited: many existing datasets are small [ 90 , 2 , 50 , 32 , 75 ] , which has prevented models from reaching the robustness and accuracy required for routine clinical use. Second, existing biomarkers may lack sufficient expressivity to capture the biology that determines NAT response. These include genomic assays (e.g., HER2DX [ 86 ] ), receptor status (estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), HER2) [ 59 ] , and histological features such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) [ 26 , 25 , 44 , 57 , 71 , 98 , 69 ] . Within HR + + /HER2 − - patients, pCR rates vary with gene-expression scores [ 37 ] , motivating richer characterization of response-relevant biology beyond receptor status alone. Transcriptome-wide analyses indicate that molecular read-outs of the tumor phenotype may be informative for predicting NAT response [ 14 , 38 ] , but such research-grade assays are not clinically deployable at scale, and clinical RNA-based tests measure only small lists of targets (typically <100 genes [ 86 ] ). Histological features fare no better: TILs track response across subtypes but stratify coarsely [ 26 , 25 , 44 , 57 , 71 , 98 , 69 ] . Third, assessments themselves can be unstable, for two reasons: tumor sampling bias and observer variability. Needle biopsies typically sample less than one percent of the tumor bulk [ 64 ] . As breast tumors are heterogeneous ecosystems of malignant cells and their microenvironment [ 72 ] , this gives rise to tumor sampling bias [ 11 ] . When the genes of five gene expression assays were measured across matched regions of the same tumor, a quarter of patients crossed a risk-category boundary depending on which region was assayed [ 43 ] . Additionally, manual assessments add observer variability: scoring of TILs and Ki-67 is only moderately reproducible between observers and laboratories [ 60 , 85 ] . Stability to sampling is a prerequisite for a biopsy-based biomarker, yet it is seldom reported. Deep learning applied to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images offers a route to prediction that requires no additional tissue, molecular assay, or manual read. Foundation models—neural networks pretrained by self-supervised learning on millions of unlabeled tissue images [ 15 , 10 , 19 , 110 , 107 ] —convert any H&E slide into rich morphological representations (embeddings) without large annotated datasets. Turning those representations into a predictor of a clinical endpoint, however, still requires many labeled patients, and NAT cohorts with recorded response are small. Due to the large quantity and high dimensionality of pathology embeddings and the small NAT cohorts, we reasoned that dividing this learning problem into two stages could help: relating morphology to tumor biology, then relating that biology to treatment response. Existing pan-cancer cohorts pair each patient’s slides with a measured transcriptome—thousands of quantitative measurements per patient rather than one binary label. These paired data can teach a model how morphology relates to molecular features. Gene expression is also a useful intermediate representation because it both shapes treatment response and leaves visible traces in tissue morphology [ 91 , 48 , 83 ] . Learning to infer expression from these larger cohorts could leave the smaller NAT cohorts with the simpler task of relating inferred molecular features to response. Therefore, we built an AI model to infer gene expression from morphology and another AI model to predict pCR from the inferred expression [ 48 , 14 ] , rather than a single model to predict response directly from the slide. This design draws on broad transcriptional information without requiring an additional molecular assay or relying on a narrowly selected gene list, and yields an interpretable representation that can be related to NAT response biology. Here we present Ataraxis Breast NEO (hereafter NEO), a multi-modal AI model that estimates the probability of pCR from a pre-treatment biopsy H&E slide together with baseline clinical variables ( Figure 1 a). Its first step, MORPHEUS (Morphological Oncology Representation and Prediction of High-dimensional Expression Using Slides), is a pan-cancer model developed on 8,742 patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) [ 47 ] spanning 32 projects to infer the expression of 14,773 genes from morphology alone. Its second step predicts pCR from that inferred expression with the standard clinical variables. NEO was developed on 1,080 patients from five cohorts and evaluated on 1,412 patients from nine independent cohorts. We assessed four aspects: discrimination relative to benchmarks, added value beyond the clinical variables, explainability of the predictions, and stability to biopsy sampling. Five cohorts from three countries (Gundersen, Omica, TransNEO [ 90 ] , Yale [ 33 ] and NYU; N = 1,080) were used for development and nine independent cohorts from five countries (Protege, UChicago [ 49 ] , Nexus [ 103 ] , Dordrecht, IMPRESS [ 50 ] , Jagiellonian, Shaare Zedek, Providence [ 8 ] , and Łódź; N = 1,412) for evaluation, spanning diverse molecular subtypes and geographies. Of the development cohorts, Omica, Gundersen, and NYU were used for cross-validation (hereafter cross-validation cohorts), and TransNEO and Yale for training only ( Section 4.7 ). Cohort characteristics are given in Table 1 . The evaluation set ( Table 2 ), used for all reported pCR performance estimates, had an overall pCR rate of 37.3% and a near-even split across the molecular subtypes (36.7% TNBC, 31.5% HR + + /HER2 − - , 30.8% HER2 + + ). The label used for model development and evaluation was pCR, assessed at surgery as the absence of residual invasive disease in both the breast and regional lymph nodes, consistent with the NeoSTEEP definition [ 65 ] ( Section 4.1 ). As the evaluation cohorts differ in size, subtype composition, and pCR rate ( Figure 1 b), performance is pooled with a random-effects model throughout ( Section 4.9 ). This heterogeneity reflects real population differences, enabling a stronger assessment of generalizability. In total, the imaging data comprise 3,606 pre-treatment biopsy slides carrying 19.6 million 224 × \times 224-pixel tissue patches (median 4,123 per slide; Figure 1 c). The model operates in two steps. First, MORPHEUS infers expression values for 14,773 protein-coding genes from the WSIs, referred to here as H&E-inferred expression ( Figure 1 e). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.03651 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Oct 2026] Title: MRVQ: One Resident Index for Dimension- and Rate-Elastic Vector Search Authors: Sean Culatana , Shang-En Huang , Kang Li View a PDF of the paper titled MRVQ: One Resident Index for Dimension- and Rate-Elastic Vector Search, by Sean Culatana and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Dense-retrieval services must switch among embedding-prefix dimensions and index bit rates as latency, quality, and memory budgets change. Tuning a quantizer separately for each rate gives the best quality, but the retrieval tier then holds several code streams and quantizer states at once. We introduce Matryoshka Residual Vector Quantization (MRVQ), a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings. Its maximum-rate code can be truncated two ways: dropping residual stages lowers the rate, and dropping embedding coordinates lowers the dimension. One resident artifact therefore serves every (dimension, rate) pair we evaluate. Across FiQA and NFCorpus, four embedding families, and {4, 8, 16}-byte codes, MRVQ is the lowest-RAM design we evaluate. It uses 17.8-22.0x less memory than three separately trained QINCo2 indices, and 1.89-2.02x less than a lean shared-model steelman. The saving is not free: per-rate QINCo2 is 0.026-0.107 nDCG@10 better on FiQA. But MRVQ beats PQ, OPQ, and AdANNS-OPQ at matched code size. We also evaluate a low-build-cost PCA-scalar design that attains quality comparable to RaBitQ and its extension while fitting 420x faster at the median. Finally, we report two negative results: QINCo2 collapses when trained at high rates, and a ranking-bound hypothesis misses its pre-specified acceptance criteria. MRVQ is therefore a low-memory operating point for elastic retrieval, not a universal quality winner. items.content: \workshoptitle NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Machine Learning for Systems (MLForSys) MRVQ: One Resident Index for Dimension- and Rate-Elastic Vector Search Sean Culatana Affiliation: Atlassian Affiliation: Mountain View, CA Email: sculatana@atlassian.com Shang-En Huang Affiliation: National Taiwan University Affiliation: Taipei, Taiwan Email: sehuang@csie.ntu.edu.tw Kang Li Affiliation: Atlassian Affiliation: Bellevue, WA Email: kli3@atlassian.com Abstract Dense-retrieval services must switch among embedding-prefix dimensions and index bit rates as latency, quality, and memory budgets change. Tuning a quantizer separately for each rate gives the best quality, but the retrieval tier then holds several code streams and quantizer states at once. We introduce Matryoshka Residual Vector Quantization (MRVQ) , a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings. Its maximum-rate code can be truncated two ways: dropping residual stages lowers the rate, and dropping embedding coordinates lowers the dimension. One resident artifact therefore serves every (dimension, rate) pair we evaluate. Across FiQA and NFCorpus, four embedding families, and { 4 , 8 , 16 } \{4,8,16\} -byte codes, MRVQ is the lowest-RAM design we evaluate. It uses 17.8 17.8 – 22.0 × 22.0\times less memory than three separately trained QINCo2 indices, and 1.89 1.89 – 2.02 × 2.02\times less than a lean shared-model steelman. The saving is not free: per-rate QINCo2 is 0.026 0.026 – 0.107 0.107 nDCG@10 better on FiQA. But MRVQ beats PQ, OPQ, and AdANNS-OPQ at matched code size. We also evaluate a low-build-cost PCA-scalar design that attains quality comparable to RaBitQ and its extension while fitting 420 × 420\times faster at the median. Finally, we report two negative results: QINCo2 collapses when trained at high rates, and a ranking-bound hypothesis misses its pre-specified acceptance criteria. MRVQ is therefore a low-memory operating point for elastic retrieval, not a universal quality winner. 1 Introduction Dense retrieval is a first-class component of retrieval-augmented generation and agentic systems. For large corpora, the document embeddings and index state—rather than the query encoder—often dominate resident memory: a 768 768 – 1024 1024 dimensional fp32 vector occupies 3 3 – 4 4 KB before indexing. That state must also support more than one operating point. Dimension elasticity uses prefixes of Matryoshka representations to trade retrieval quality for query compute and bandwidth ( Kusupati et al., 2022 ; Rege et al., 2023 ) ; rate elasticity changes the document code size to trade quality for storage. A high-quality deployment can tune a quantizer independently for each rate, but then the retrieval tier retains several code streams and model states at once. We ask whether a single resident document code can cover both axes. MRVQ fits a residual vector quantizer post-hoc on frozen embeddings, weighting reconstruction error across the served prefix dimensions. Residual stages provide nested rates, and coordinate prefixes provide nested dimensions, so the same stored code supports every ( m , b ) ∈ ℳ × ℬ (m,b)\in\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{B} (Figure 1 ). This differs from AdANNS, which targets dimension-adaptive search, and from MatQuant, which nests model-weight precision rather than document-index codes ( Nair et al., 2025 ) ; Appendix E places MRVQ among quantizers for approximate search. Our contribution is a systems trade-off, not a claim of universal quality dominance. First, we formalize resident-memory accounting for a full rate menu and show that one MRVQ artifact is the lowest-RAM configuration evaluated. Second, we measure the corresponding quality cost against QINCo2 and the gains over standard ANN quantizers. Third, we evaluate a separate, inexpensive PCA-scalar design for hosts on which iterative quantizer training is undesirable. Finally, we report two negative results—high-rate QINCo2 training failures and a ranking-preservation predictor that does not meet our pre-specified bar. Figure 1: Amortizing a rate-and-dimension menu. A rate-specialized deployment keeps one quantizer state and one code stream per rate; each stream may still expose every embedding-prefix dimension. MRVQ stores one maximum-rate residual code: stage prefixes select 4 / 8 / 16 4/8/16 B/vector, and coordinate prefixes select the embedding dimension. The document-code term falls from 28 ​ n 28n to 16 ​ n 16n bytes, and sharing the quantizer state produces the larger measured saving (Table 1 ). Quoted totals are FiQA at D = 768 D\!=\!768 . 2 MRVQ and Resident-Memory Model Let { x i } i = 1 n ⊂ ℝ D \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} be frozen document embeddings. An L L -stage residual vector quantizer with K = 256 K=256 codewords per stage produces indices z i ( 1 : L ) z_{i}^{(1:L)} and reconstructions x ^ i ( ℓ ) = ∑ j = 1 ℓ C z i ( j ) ( j ) \hat{x}_{i}^{(\ell)}=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}C^{(j)}_{z_{i}^{(j)}} . Because each stage index occupies one byte, decoding the first b b stages gives a b b -byte code. MRVQ makes the same code dimension-elastic by fitting the codebooks under ℒ prefix = ∑ i = 1 n ∑ m ∈ ℳ w m ‖ x i [ : m ] − x ^ i ( L ) [ : m ] ‖ 2 2 , w m ≥ 0 , ∑ m w m = 1 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prefix}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}w_{m}\left\|x_{i}^{[:m]}-\hat{x}_{i}^{(L)[:m]}\right\|_{2}^{2},\qquad w_{m}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{m}w_{m}=1. (1) At serving time, ( m , b ) (m,b) selects x ^ i ( b ) [ : m ] \hat{x}_{i}^{(b)[:m]} ; no re-encoding and no additional document code is required. Queries remain in floating point and are scored asymmetrically, as in PQ/OPQ and RaBitQ. For the evaluated L = 16 L=16 , MRVQ’s resident state is R MRVQ = 4 ​ L ​ K ​ D + 16 ​ n R_{\mathrm{MRVQ}}=4LKD+16n bytes: fp32 codebooks plus one 16 16 -byte code per vector. A deployment with a separate QINCo2 artifact for each b ∈ ℬ = { 4 , 8 , 16 } b\in\mathcal{B}=\{4,8,16\} costs R sep = ∑ b ∈ ℬ ( P b + n ​ b ) R_{\mathrm{sep}}=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}(P_{b}+nb) , where P b P_{b} is the corresponding model state; a shared-model steelman costs R shared = P 16 + 16 ​ n R_{\mathrm{shared}}=P_{16}+16n . The document-code term alone therefore changes from 28 ​ n 28n to 16 ​ n 16n bytes ( 1.75 × 1.75\times asymptotically), and at the corpus sizes we evaluate, sharing the fixed quantizer state produces a much larger ratio. Appendix A reports the fixed and per-vector terms separately so the accounting can be checked at any n n . We also study a separate PCA-scalar operating point: rotate by PCA, allocate scalar bits by coordinate variance, and quantize each coordinate independently. It requires an eigendecomposition but no iterative learned-codebook training; it is not included in the MRVQ memory accounting. 3 Evaluation We use FiQA ( 57,638 57{,}638 documents, 648 648 queries) and NFCorpus ( 3,633 3{,}633 documents, 323 323 queries) from BEIR ( Thakur et al., 2021 ) . The four embedding families are MPNet ( Reimers and Gurevych, 2019 ) ( D = 768 D=768 ), Mxbai ( Lee et al., 2024 ) ( D = 1024 D=1024 ), Nomic ( Nussbaum et al., 2024 ) ( D = 768 D=768 ), and BGE ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) ( D = 768 D=768 ). Within each family, every method uses the same fixed, model-specific prefix menu ℳ ⊆ { 128,256,384,512,768 , 1024 } \mathcal{M}\subseteq\{128,256,384,512,768,1024\} , and a “menu mean” is the unweighted mean over that family’s evaluated prefix-rate cells. The prefix weights w m w_{m} in Eq. ( 1 ) are uniform over ℳ \mathcal{M} and all 16 16 residual stages are weighted equally; Appendix F lists the exact checkpoints, menus, and fitting budget. Rates are ℬ = { 4 , 8 , 16 } \mathcal{B}=\{4,8,16\} B/vector, or 192 192 – 1024 × 1024\times smaller than the corresponding fp32 vector before fixed quantizer overhead. The metric is nDCG@10. Learned baselines use matched fitting budgets, and their aggregated per-rate results reproduce the stored runs to floating-point tolerance (maximum absolute deviation 0 0 for MRVQ, 5 × 10 − 17 5\times 10^{-17} for QINCo2). We use paired per-query bootstrap confidence intervals ( 5000 5000 resamples; 10,000 10{,}000 for the RaBitQ study). Decision thresholds for the negative-result tests were fixed before the final aggregate analyses. Reported RAM is analytical accounting from the byte formulas above—parameter and code bytes only, with no optimizer or runtime buffers—rather than measured process RSS. 4 Results One artifact is the low-RAM corner. Table 1 prices the complete { 4 , 8 , 16 } \{4,8,16\} B/vector menu. MRVQ uses 12.06 12.06 – 16.88 16.88 MiB and is the lowest-RAM configuration for all four families on both datasets. Relative to three separate QINCo2 models, the saving is 17.8 17.8 – 22.0 × 22.0\times ; relative to the leanest shared-model configuration (including reduced embedding width and fp16 variants), it is 1.89 1.89 – 2.02 × 2.02\times . The first ratio is largest at these on-device and per-tenant corpus scales because neural parameter state dominates the resident footprint (Appendix A ). As n n grows, the separate-model ratio approaches the 28 / 16 = 1.75 × 28/16=1.75\times code-stream ratio, while the shared-model gap becomes a fixed overhead and therefore less important; Figure 2 (b) makes both limits explicit. Table 1: Resident RAM (MiB) for the complete { 4 , 8 , 16 } \{4,8,16\} B/vector menu; ratios are relative to MRVQ. “Separate” retains one QINCo2 model and code stream per rate; “shared” is the leanest single-model steelman evaluated. Families that share an embedding width share a row because the accounting depends on D D , not on the family. Dataset Family D D MRVQ QINCo2 separate QINCo2 shared FiQA MPNet/Nomic/BGE 768 12.88 228.9 ( 17.8 × 17.8\times ) 25.17 ( 1.95 × 1.95\times ) FiQA Mxbai 1024 16.88 354.6 ( 21.0 × 21.0\times ) 31.85 ( 1.89 × 1.89\times ) NFCorpus MPNet/Nomic/BGE 768 12.06 227.4 ( 18.9 × 18.9\times ) 24.34 ( 2.02 × 2.02\times ) NFCorpus Mxbai 1024 16.06 353.2 ( 22.0 × 22.0\times ) 31.03 ( 1.93 × 1.93\times ) Figure 2: (a) FiQA menu-mean nDCG@10 versus resident RAM for the full menu. MRVQ ( ∘ \circ ) occupies the low-memory corner and per-rate QINCo2 ( □ \square ) the high-quality corner; neither dominates on both axes. The dashed line marks the leanest shared-model QINCo2 RAM, whose quality we do not measure. (b) The same accounting as a function of corpus size at D = 768 D\!=\!768 . The advantage over per-rate QINCo2 decays from ∼ \sim 18 × 18\times at the evaluated corpora to the 1.75 × 1.75\times code-stream asymptote, and the shared-model advantage falls below 1.1 × 1.1\times at n = 7.3 n\!=\!7.3 M ( ▼ \blacktriangledown ). Quality forms a two-corner Pareto. At matched code size, separately trained QINCo2 ( Huijben et al., 2024 ; Vallaeys et al., 2025 ) beats MRVQ in every FiQA family-rate cell by 0.026 0.026 – 0.107 0.107 nDCG@10 (Appendix B ). Conversely, even the shared-model QINCo2 steelman uses roughly 1.9 × 1.9\times MRVQ’s RAM at the evaluated corpus sizes. Figure 2 (a) therefore shows two useful operating points rather than a single winner. The low-memory result repeats on NFCorpus for all four families. Against standard fixed-code ANN baselines, MRVQ is stronger at matched bytes. Across the aggressive 4 4 – 16 16 B/vector regime, paired-bootstrap intervals favor MRVQ over per-prefix OPQ by about 0.06 0.06 – 0.07 0.07 nDCG@10, over PQ by 0.10 0.10 – 0.12 0.12 , and over AdANNS-OPQ ( Rege et al., 2023 ) in every evaluated cell. The practical rule is therefore constraint-dependent: choose QINCo2 when quality dominates, and MRVQ when resident memory prevents keeping several specialized artifacts. A low-build-cost scalar alternative. We compare PCA-scalar with RaBitQ and Extended-RaBitQ ( Gao and Long, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024 ) using native Faiss 1.13.2 asymmetric cosine search on ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized vectors. At nominal b ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 } b\in\{1,2,4\} bits/dimension, the RaBitQ representation receives an additional 8 / 20 / 20 8/20/20 B/vector, so the byte accounting is conservative for PCA-scalar. Across the two aggregate query grids, pooled PCA-scalar − - RaBitQ deltas are + 0.0076 / + 0.0029 / + 0.0010 +0.0076/+0.0029/+0.0010 and − 0.0009 / + 0.0012 / + 0.0006 -0.0009/+0.0012/+0.0006 nDCG@10 at b = 1 / 2 / 4 b=1/2/4 . All absolute effects are below 0.008 0.008 , and one Mxbai 1 1 -bit cell favors RaBitQ by 0.0039 0.0039 ; we therefore describe quality as comparable, not superior. Timed separately on three held-out BEIR corpora ( 18 18 cells, fixed 8 8 -thread CPU), PCA training is 420 × 420\times faster than matched OPQ fitting at the median and 686 × 686\times at the mean, with a 47 47 – 1967 × 1967\times spread: 0.17 0.17 – 6.95 6.95 s against 72 72 – 416 416 s. That makes it attractive for in-place rebuilds (Appendix C ). 5 Limitations and Conclusion Training reliability. On NFCorpus at 16 16 stages, per-rate QINCo2 suffers retrieval collapse—nDCG@10 below half the MRVQ value despite converged validation MSE—in 3 / 3 3/3 BGE seeds (best 0.035 0.035 ) and 1 / 3 1/3 Nomic seeds. The best surviving Nomic seed is also non-monotone in rate: 0.294 0.294 at 16 16 stages against 0.320 0.320 at 8 8 . We retain these failures rather than silently dropping them. No ranking certificate. A parameter-free predictor based on residual energy is directionally useful but misses our pre-specified acceptance bar: pooled rank correlation is 0.825 0.825 against a required 0.85 0.85 , and only 72 % 72\% of cells yield a non-vacuous bound against a required 90 % 90\% (Appendix D ). Scope. The quality study covers two modest BEIR corpora and four embedding families. We measure resident memory and ranking quality, not end-to-end ANN latency, build energy, or recall–throughput curves; the RAM gains should not be read as speedups. At very large n n the advantage over a shared-model baseline narrows as the accounting predicts. Within that scope, MRVQ converts a dimension-and-rate menu from several rate-specialized resident artifacts into one post-hoc code. It pays a measurable quality cost to QINCo2, but beats standard ANN quantizers at matched bytes and occupies a distinct low-memory Pareto point. That is the intended systems contribution: a simple deployment option for elastic retrieval when resident memory, rather than peak quality, is the binding resource. items.raw_text: \workshoptitle NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Machine Learning for Systems (MLForSys) MRVQ: One Resident Index for Dimension- and Rate-Elastic Vector Search Sean Culatana Affiliation: Atlassian Affiliation: Mountain View, CA Email: sculatana@atlassian.com Shang-En Huang Affiliation: National Taiwan University Affiliation: Taipei, Taiwan Email: sehuang@csie.ntu.edu.tw Kang Li Affiliation: Atlassian Affiliation: Bellevue, WA Email: kli3@atlassian.com Abstract Dense-retrieval services must switch among embedding-prefix dimensions and index bit rates as latency, quality, and memory budgets change. Tuning a quantizer separately for each rate gives the best quality, but the retrieval tier then holds several code streams and quantizer states at once. We introduce Matryoshka Residual Vector Quantization (MRVQ) , a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings. Its maximum-rate code can be truncated two ways: dropping residual stages lowers the rate, and dropping embedding coordinates lowers the dimension. One resident artifact therefore serves every (dimension, rate) pair we evaluate. Across FiQA and NFCorpus, four embedding families, and { 4 , 8 , 16 } \{4,8,16\} -byte codes, MRVQ is the lowest-RAM design we evaluate. It uses 17.8 17.8 – 22.0 × 22.0\times less memory than three separately trained QINCo2 indices, and 1.89 1.89 – 2.02 × 2.02\times less than a lean shared-model steelman. The saving is not free: per-rate QINCo2 is 0.026 0.026 – 0.107 0.107 nDCG@10 better on FiQA. But MRVQ beats PQ, OPQ, and AdANNS-OPQ at matched code size. We also evaluate a low-build-cost PCA-scalar design that attains quality comparable to RaBitQ and its extension while fitting 420 × 420\times faster at the median. Finally, we report two negative results: QINCo2 collapses when trained at high rates, and a ranking-bound hypothesis misses its pre-specified acceptance criteria. MRVQ is therefore a low-memory operating point for elastic retrieval, not a universal quality winner. 1 Introduction Dense retrieval is a first-class component of retrieval-augmented generation and agentic systems. For large corpora, the document embeddings and index state—rather than the query encoder—often dominate resident memory: a 768 768 – 1024 1024 dimensional fp32 vector occupies 3 3 – 4 4 KB before indexing. That state must also support more than one operating point. Dimension elasticity uses prefixes of Matryoshka representations to trade retrieval quality for query compute and bandwidth ( Kusupati et al., 2022 ; Rege et al., 2023 ) ; rate elasticity changes the document code size to trade quality for storage. A high-quality deployment can tune a quantizer independently for each rate, but then the retrieval tier retains several code streams and model states at once. We ask whether a single resident document code can cover both axes. MRVQ fits a residual vector quantizer post-hoc on frozen embeddings, weighting reconstruction error across the served prefix dimensions. Residual stages provide nested rates, and coordinate prefixes provide nested dimensions, so the same stored code supports every ( m , b ) ∈ ℳ × ℬ (m,b)\in\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{B} (Figure 1 ). This differs from AdANNS, which targets dimension-adaptive search, and from MatQuant, which nests model-weight precision rather than document-index codes ( Nair et al., 2025 ) ; Appendix E places MRVQ among quantizers for approximate search. Our contribution is a systems trade-off, not a claim of universal quality dominance. First, we formalize resident-memory accounting for a full rate menu and show that one MRVQ artifact is the lowest-RAM configuration evaluated. Second, we measure the corresponding quality cost against QINCo2 and the gains over standard ANN quantizers. Third, we evaluate a separate, inexpensive PCA-scalar design for hosts on which iterative quantizer training is undesirable. Finally, we report two negative results—high-rate QINCo2 training failures and a ranking-preservation predictor that does not meet our pre-specified bar. Figure 1: Amortizing a rate-and-dimension menu. A rate-specialized deployment keeps one quantizer state and one code stream per rate; each stream may still expose every embedding-prefix dimension. MRVQ stores one maximum-rate residual code: stage prefixes select 4 / 8 / 16 4/8/16 B/vector, and coordinate prefixes select the embedding dimension. The document-code term falls from 28 ​ n 28n to 16 ​ n 16n bytes, and sharing the quantizer state produces the larger measured saving (Table 1 ). Quoted totals are FiQA at D = 768 D\!=\!768 . 2 MRVQ and Resident-Memory Model Let { x i } i = 1 n ⊂ ℝ D \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} be frozen document embeddings. Queries remain in floating point and are scored asymmetrically, as in PQ/OPQ and RaBitQ. For the evaluated L = 16 L=16 , MRVQ’s resident state is R MRVQ = 4 ​ L ​ K ​ D + 16 ​ n R_{\mathrm{MRVQ}}=4LKD+16n bytes: fp32 codebooks plus one 16 16 -byte code per vector. A deployment with a separate QINCo2 artifact for each b ∈ ℬ = { 4 , 8 , 16 } b\in\mathcal{B}=\{4,8,16\} costs R sep = ∑ b ∈ ℬ ( P b + n ​ b ) R_{\mathrm{sep}}=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}(P_{b}+nb) , where P b P_{b} is the corresponding model state; a shared-model steelman costs R shared = P 16 + 16 ​ n R_{\mathrm{shared}}=P_{16}+16n . The document-code term alone therefore changes from 28 ​ n 28n to 16 ​ n 16n bytes ( 1.75 × 1.75\times asymptotically), and at the corpus sizes we evaluate, sharing the fixed quantizer state produces a much larger ratio. Appendix A reports the fixed and per-vector terms separately so the accounting can be checked at any n n . We also study a separate PCA-scalar operating point: rotate by PCA, allocate scalar bits by coordinate variance, and quantize each coordinate independently. It requires an eigendecomposition but no iterative learned-codebook training; it is not included in the MRVQ memory accounting. 3 Evaluation We use FiQA ( 57,638 57{,}638 documents, 648 648 queries) and NFCorpus ( 3,633 3{,}633 documents, 323 323 queries) from BEIR ( Thakur et al., 2021 ) . The four embedding families are MPNet ( Reimers and Gurevych, 2019 ) ( D = 768 D=768 ), Mxbai ( Lee et al., 2024 ) ( D = 1024 D=1024 ), Nomic ( Nussbaum et al., 2024 ) ( D = 768 D=768 ), and BGE ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) ( D = 768 D=768 ). Within each family, every method uses the same fixed, model-specific prefix menu ℳ ⊆ { 128,256,384,512,768 , 1024 } \mathcal{M}\subseteq\{128,256,384,512,768,1024\} , and a “menu mean” is the unweighted mean over that family’s evaluated prefix-rate cells. The prefix weights w m w_{m} in Eq. ( 1 ) are uniform over ℳ \mathcal{M} and all 16 16 residual stages are weighted equally; Appendix F lists the exact checkpoints, menus, and fitting budget. Rates are ℬ = { 4 , 8 , 16 } \mathcal{B}=\{4,8,16\} B/vector, or 192 192 – 1024 × 1024\times smaller than the corresponding fp32 vector before fixed quantizer overhead. The metric is nDCG@10. Learned baselines use matched fitting budgets, and their aggregated per-rate results reproduce the stored runs to floating-point tolerance (maximum absolute deviation 0 0 for MRVQ, 5 × 10 − 17 5\times 10^{-17} for QINCo2). We use paired per-query bootstrap confidence intervals ( 5000 5000 resamples; 10,000 10{,}000 for the RaBitQ study). Decision thresholds for the negative-result tests were fixed before the final aggregate analyses. Reported RAM is analytical accounting from the byte formulas above—parameter and code bytes only, with no optimizer or runtime buffers—rather than measured process RSS. 4 Results One artifact is the low-RAM corner. Table 1 prices the complete { 4 , 8 , 16 } \{4,8,16\} B/vector menu. MRVQ uses 12.06 12.06 – 16.88 16.88 MiB and is the lowest-RAM configuration for all four families on both datasets. Relative to three separate QINCo2 models, the saving is 17.8 17.8 – 22.0 × 22.0\times ; relative to the leanest shared-model configuration (including reduced embedding width and fp16 variants), it is 1.89 1.89 – 2.02 × 2.02\times . The first ratio is largest at these on-device and per-tenant corpus scales because neural parameter state dominates the resident footprint (Appendix A ). As n n grows, the separate-model ratio approaches the 28 / 16 = 1.75 × 28/16=1.75\times code-stream ratio, while the shared-model gap becomes a fixed overhead and therefore less important; Figure 2 (b) makes both limits explicit. MRVQ ( ∘ \circ ) occupies the low-memory corner and per-rate QINCo2 ( □ \square ) the high-quality corner; neither dominates on both axes. The dashed line marks the leanest shared-model QINCo2 RAM, whose quality we do not measure. (b) The same accounting as a function of corpus size at D = 768 D\!=\!768 . The advantage over per-rate QINCo2 decays from ∼ \sim 18 × 18\times at the evaluated corpora to the 1.75 × 1.75\times code-stream asymptote, and the shared-model advantage falls below 1.1 × 1.1\times at n = 7.3 n\!=\!7.3 M ( ▼ \blacktriangledown ). Quality forms a two-corner Pareto. At matched code size, separately trained QINCo2 ( Huijben et al., 2024 ; Vallaeys et al., 2025 ) beats MRVQ in every FiQA family-rate cell by 0.026 0.026 – 0.107 0.107 nDCG@10 (Appendix B ). Conversely, even the shared-model QINCo2 steelman uses roughly 1.9 × 1.9\times MRVQ’s RAM at the evaluated corpus sizes. Figure 2 (a) therefore shows two useful operating points rather than a single winner. The low-memory result repeats on NFCorpus for all four families. Against standard fixed-code ANN baselines, MRVQ is stronger at matched bytes. Across the aggressive 4 4 – 16 16 B/vector regime, paired-bootstrap intervals favor MRVQ over per-prefix OPQ by about 0.06 0.06 – 0.07 0.07 nDCG@10, over PQ by 0.10 0.10 – 0.12 0.12 , and over AdANNS-OPQ ( Rege et al., 2023 ) in every evaluated cell. The practical rule is therefore constraint-dependent: choose QINCo2 when quality dominates, and MRVQ when resident memory prevents keeping several specialized artifacts. A low-build-cost scalar alternative. We compare PCA-scalar with RaBitQ and Extended-RaBitQ ( Gao and Long, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024 ) using native Faiss 1.13.2 asymmetric cosine search on ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized vectors. At nominal b ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 } b\in\{1,2,4\} bits/dimension, the RaBitQ representation receives an additional 8 / 20 / 20 8/20/20 B/vector, so the byte accounting is conservative for PCA-scalar. Across the two aggregate query grids, pooled PCA-scalar − - RaBitQ deltas are + 0.0076 / + 0.0029 / + 0.0010 +0.0076/+0.0029/+0.0010 and − 0.0009 / + 0.0012 / + 0.0006 -0.0009/+0.0012/+0.0006 nDCG@10 at b = 1 / 2 / 4 b=1/2/4 . All absolute effects are below 0.008 0.008 , and one Mxbai 1 1 -bit cell favors RaBitQ by 0.0039 0.0039 ; we therefore describe quality as comparable, not superior. Timed separately on three held-out BEIR corpora ( 18 18 cells, fixed 8 8 -thread CPU), PCA training is 420 × 420\times faster than matched OPQ fitting at the median and 686 × 686\times at the mean, with a 47 47 – 1967 × 1967\times spread: 0.17 0.17 – 6.95 6.95 s against 72 72 – 416 416 s. That makes it attractive for in-place rebuilds (Appendix C ). 5 Limitations and Conclusion Training reliability. On NFCorpus at 16 16 stages, per-rate QINCo2 suffers retrieval collapse—nDCG@10 below half the MRVQ value despite converged validation MSE—in 3 / 3 3/3 BGE seeds (best 0.035 0.035 ) and 1 / 3 1/3 Nomic seeds. The best surviving Nomic seed is also non-monotone in rate: 0.294 0.294 at 16 16 stages against 0.320 0.320 at 8 8 . We retain these failures rather than silently dropping them. No ranking certificate. A parameter-free predictor based on residual energy is directionally useful but misses our pre-specified acceptance bar: pooled rank correlation is 0.825 0.825 against a required 0.85 0.85 , and only 72 % 72\% of cells yield a non-vacuous bound against a required 90 % 90\% (Appendix D ). Scope. The quality study covers two modest BEIR corpora and four embedding families. We measure resident memory and ranking quality, not end-to-end ANN latency, build energy, or recall–throughput curves; the RAM gains should not be read as speedups. At very large n n the advantage over a shared-model baseline narrows as the accounting predicts. Within that scope, MRVQ converts a dimension-and-rate menu from several rate-specialized resident artifacts into one post-hoc code. It pays a measurable quality cost to QINCo2, but beats standard ANN quantizers at matched bytes and occupies a distinct low-memory Pareto point. That is the intended systems contribution: a simple deployment option for elastic retrieval when resident memory, rather than peak quality, is the binding resource. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.03639 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Oct 2026] Title: Do Large Language Models Know Colombian Law? A Reliability Benchmark for the Colombian Legal System Authors: Rubén Manrique , Michelle Castellanos , Jorge Morales , Juan David Gutiérrez , Antonio Barreto Rozo , Joaquín Vélez Navarro View a PDF of the paper titled Do Large Language Models Know Colombian Law? A Reliability Benchmark for the Colombian Legal System, by Rub\'en Manrique and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support legal practice, education, and research, yet their reliability in national legal systems outside the United States remains largely undocumented. We introduce an expert-validated benchmark for evaluating LLM reliability on the Colombian legal system. The benchmark comprises 1,042 items spanning ten areas of law and three question formats (closed multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended IRAC), built through a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review. We evaluate 15 contemporary proprietary and open-weight models with format-appropriate metrics. Accuracy on closed questions ranges widely, from 0.905 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to 0.577, but on free-text legal answers factual correctness never exceeds 0.45 (on a 0-1 scale) for any model. We find a dissociation between answer relevancy and correctness (Spearman rho = -0.46): models reliably sound responsive while frequently being wrong, a pattern of particular concern for non-expert users. Closed-question accuracy and free-text correctness are strongly rank-correlated (rho = 0.94), so cheap multiple-choice screening predicts model ranking but overstates absolute reliability. An independent rubric-based LLM judge and blind human expert scoring both reproduce the free-text ranking (rho >= 0.88). The judge further reveals that only about half of the norms models cite are correct; the rest are wrong or non-existent. Reliability varies systematically by legal area and follows an inverted-U across question complexity. Our results indicate that current LLMs require expert supervision for Colombian legal tasks, and that grounding answers in authoritative sources is a promising path to higher reliability. We release the benchmark construction pipeline to support reproducible evaluation. items.content: Do Large Language Models Know Colombian Law? A Reliability Benchmark for the Colombian Legal System Rubén Manrique Michelle Castellanos Jorge Morales Juan David Gutiérrez Antonio Barreto Rozo Joaquín Vélez Navarro 1 Department of Systems and Computing Engineering, Universidad de los Andes 2 School of Government, Universidad de los Andes 3 Faculty of Law, Universidad de los Andes October 2, 2026 Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support legal practice, education, and research, yet their reliability in national legal systems outside the United States remains largely undocumented. We introduce an expert-validated benchmark for evaluating LLM reliability on the Colombian legal system. The benchmark comprises 1042 1042 items spanning ten areas of law and three question formats—closed single-best-answer multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended (IRAC)—built through a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review. We evaluate 15 15 contemporary proprietary and open-weight models, scoring each question format with format-appropriate metrics. Accuracy on closed questions ranges widely, from 0.905 0.905 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to 0.577 0.577 ; but on free-text legal answers, factual correctness never exceeds 0.45 0.45 for any model. Both metrics range from 0 0 to 1 1 , where 1 1 denotes a perfect score. We find a dissociation between answer relevancy and correctness (Spearman ρ = − 0.46 \rho=-0.46 ), so that models reliably sound responsive while frequently being wrong , a pattern of particular concern for non-expert users. Closed-question accuracy and free-text correctness are strongly rank-correlated ( ρ = 0.94 \rho=0.94 ), so cheap multiple-choice screening predicts model ranking but overstates absolute reliability. The free-text ranking proves robust, because an independent rubric-based LLM judge and blind human expert scoring both reproduce it ( ρ ≥ 0.88 \rho\geq 0.88 ). That judge, validated against the human experts, further reveals that the norms models cite are frequently unreliable—only about half are correct, and the rest cite the wrong norm or one that does not exist. Reliability varies systematically by legal area and follows an inverted-U across question complexity. Our results indicate that current LLMs require expert supervision for Colombian legal tasks, and that grounding answers in authoritative sources is a promising path to higher reliability. We release the benchmark construction pipeline to support reproducible evaluation. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have moved quickly from novelty to a working tool in the legal profession. A 2023 UNESCO global survey found that 40 40 % of surveyed judges, lawyers, and other judicial operators had already used ChatGPT or similar tools for work, most often to search for legal information (case law, statutes, doctrine) and to draft documents [ 11 ] . No comparable survey exists for Colombia, but the Consejo Superior de la Judicatura 1 1 1 The Consejo Superior de la Judicatura is the body in charge of administering the Colombian judicial branch. found that roughly one in three of the 3152 3152 judicial employees it surveyed had used AI systems, ChatGPT being the most common [ 3 ] . Adoption, in short, is already widespread and largely unsupervised. These tools, however, exhibit a well-documented failure mode. LLMs hallucinate , producing fluent but incorrect or fabricated legal content [ 4 ] . Lawyers and judges in several countries have pasted tool-generated text—including citations to non-existent statutes and case law—into briefs and judicial decisions without verification [ 10 , 12 ] . Empirical studies in the United States quantify the risk. General-purpose models such as GPT-4 hallucinate on more than half of legal queries and struggle to recognize their own errors [ 4 ] , and even commercial tools marketed as “hallucination-free,” such as Lexis+ AI and Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, answer incorrectly between 17 17 % and 33 33 % of the time despite using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [ 14 ] . Almost all of this evidence concerns English-language, U.S. common law. Empirical research on LLM reliability in Spanish-speaking, civil-law jurisdictions—and on Colombian law in particular—remains scarce; a recent systematic review finds no dedicated Spanish-language legal QA benchmark for Latin America [ 15 ] . The gap matters because linguistic, terminological, and normative differences mean that findings obtained in English do not transfer automatically to Spanish legal practice, and commercial AI systems are not typically representative of Latin American legal diversity. The one prior assessment for Colombia concluded that, as of 2024, no evaluated model reached an accuracy acceptable for practical legal use [ 1 ] , but it predates the current generation of frontier models and covered a very limited set of areas and question types. We address this gap with a systematic, expert-validated evaluation of LLM reliability on the Colombian legal system. Our contributions are: • An expert-validated Colombian legal benchmark of 1042 1042 items spanning ten areas of law and three question formats—closed single-best-answer multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended (IRAC)—built through a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review (Sections 3 – 4 ). • A reproducible evaluation of 15 15 contemporary LLMs , proprietary and open-weight, scored with format-appropriate metrics computed over explicit question subsets (Section 5 ). • An analysis of where and how models fail (Section 6 ), including a dissociation between answer relevancy and correctness—models reliably sound responsive while frequently being wrong —and a characterization of reliability by legal area and question complexity. 2 Related Work 2.1 Legal hallucinations and the reliability of LLMs A growing body of literature measures how often LLMs produce incorrect legal content. Dahl et al. [4] provide the first systematic profile of legal hallucinations in public-facing models, reporting hallucination rates above 50 50 % on a range of tasks and a typology of failure modes. Magesh et al. [14] extend this to commercial, RAG-based legal research tools, showing that “hallucination-free” claims are overstated and that error rates of 17 17 – 33 33 % persist. Complementarily, Guha et al. [8] introduce LegalBench, a collaboratively built benchmark for legal reasoning, establishing the value of task-structured, expert-informed evaluation. For open-ended legal answers, where correctness is not a single string, Salinas et al. [18] conduct a blinded study in which sixteen U.S. law professors rate LLM and peer short answers; the models are preferred over human peers, and the authors show that a separate LLM acting as a judge reproduces expert agreement, supporting LLM-as-a-judge as a scalable, expert-aligned evaluation method for judgment-rich legal tasks. Our work adopts this evaluation philosophy—and a reference-anchored LLM-judge protocol in the same spirit—but targets a non-U.S., civil-law jurisdiction and explicitly separates recognition (closed questions) from generation (free text). 2.2 AI in the Justice System in Latin America and Colombia A parallel literature documents the adoption and governance of AI in judicial and public-sector settings. Global and regional surveys map where and how judicial operators use these tools [ 11 , 3 , 6 ] , and guidance has begun to emerge on their responsible use in courts [ 12 , 9 ] . In Colombia specifically, studies have examined automated decision-making in the public sector [ 13 , 7 ] , the use of AI in the Attorney General’s Office [ 16 ] , and the Constitutional Court’s PretorIA system for processing human-rights cases [ 17 ] . Critical appraisals caution against uncritical reliance on LLMs in judicial decision-making [ 10 , 2 ] . This body of work establishes the stakes and the demand for AI in Colombian legal practice; it motivates, but does not itself provide, a systematic measurement of how reliably current LLMs actually answer Colombian legal questions. 2.3 Spanish-language legal QA in Latin America The work that most directly motivates this benchmark is the systematic review and zero-shot evaluation of Manrique et al. [15] . Surveying 41 41 legal-NLP benchmarks published between 2018 and 2026, they find that Latin America is represented by only six—all covering Brazil and Portuguese—and that no dedicated Spanish-language legal QA benchmark exists, despite Spanish being spoken across eighteen civil-law countries in the region. They further provide a first zero-shot evaluation of five LLMs on 458 458 bar-exam-style multiple-choice questions from Bolivia, Colombia, and Puerto Rico, where the best model reaches only 79.7 79.7 % accuracy and performance is weakest in criminal and administrative law. Crucially for the present work, that study is confined to closed multiple-choice items and explicitly calls for dedicated Spanish-language legal benchmarks that go beyond the multiple-choice format and incorporate expert validation. Our benchmark is a direct response to that call: it focuses on Colombian law in depth, adds semi-open and open-ended (IRAC) formats alongside closed questions, applies a multi-stage expert-validation protocol, and evaluates a larger and more recent set of models. An earlier and narrower precedent is Arévalo-Robles and Castellanos-Cortés [1] , who evaluate three LLMs (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, and Gemini Pro) on Colombian legal queries across five areas of law and find that ChatGPT-4 performed best overall but that no model reached an acceptable level of accuracy for practical use, without releasing a reusable benchmark. Relative to both, we evaluate a larger and more diverse set of 15 15 contemporary models on an expert-validated benchmark that is larger ( 1042 1042 items), broader (ten legal areas), and stratified by question format and complexity, and we report metrics matched to each format—separating factual correctness from surface relevancy—which reveals reliability gaps that a single accuracy figure would obscure. 3 The Benchmark We evaluate LLM reliability on the Colombian Legal Reliability Benchmark , a collection of 1042 1042 expert-validated legal questions. The benchmark was designed to probe legal knowledge and reasoning at increasing levels of difficulty, following a hybrid methodology that adapts the question typologies and validation criteria of Dahl et al. [4] , Magesh et al. [14] , and Arévalo-Robles and Castellanos-Cortés [1] to the Colombian legal order. 3.1 Question taxonomy The benchmark is organized around a progressive taxonomy of three question types, each targeting a different level of legal competence and each scored with a format-appropriate metric (Section 3.4 ). Closed (single-best-answer multiple-choice) questions. Single-best-answer multiple-choice items with four mutually exclusive options that probe foundational concepts, definitions, principles, and legal classifications. Each item has exactly one correct option—the model selects one of the four, not a subset—and a documented legal basis (e.g., a specific article or ruling). These items are scored by accuracy . Semi-open questions. Items requiring a specific, concise answer (up to 150 words) about normative or conceptual content, without the constraints of multiple choice but preserving objective evaluation criteria. High -complexity items presuppose genuine legal-reasoning skills and the ability to synthesize legal information from unstructured legal texts—e.g., resolving normative conflicts, analyzing factual backgrounds, adopting a reasoned procedural stance, identifying the central legal problem and its governing basis, balancing competing principles and rights, and systematic interpretation. Level Sub-tasks Low Normative existence; competent authority; deciding judge; legal hierarchy; basic definition; legal classification; essential elements. Medium Sense of the ruling; literal reproduction of a norm; jurisprudential precedent; temporal validity; conceptual distinction; legal requirements; legal exceptions; impartiality of the judicial order. High Normative conflict; factual background; procedural stance; legal problem; central legal basis; balancing of principles and rights; systematic interpretation. Open-ended questions. Casuistic items that pose a legal problem and whose expert reference answer is written under the IRAC format— Issue , Rule , Application , and Conclusion —synthesizing the full range of legal competencies. Contributors selected the area matching their expertise, so that items are technically rigorous and representative of real practice. 3.3 Dataset composition The evaluated benchmark contains 1042 1042 items: 305 305 closed multiple-choice, 682 682 semi-open, and 55 55 open-ended questions. Figure 1 shows the composition by legal area and question type, and Table 2 reports the exact counts. Semi-open items are distributed across the three complexity levels as shown in Figure 2 ( 258 258 low, 236 236 medium, 188 188 high). Closed multiple-choice items are scored by accuracy . The platform defines four user roles with clearly delimited responsibilities: students act as content generators, producing legal questions in their area of expertise from established guidelines; a legal assistant performs primary review of the relevance, coherence, and technical quality of each item; specialized evaluators provide expert validation to guarantee legal rigor; and the technical team administers the system and configures the automated generation processes. items.raw_text: Do Large Language Models Know Colombian Law? A Reliability Benchmark for the Colombian Legal System Rubén Manrique Michelle Castellanos Jorge Morales Juan David Gutiérrez Antonio Barreto Rozo Joaquín Vélez Navarro 1 Department of Systems and Computing Engineering, Universidad de los Andes 2 School of Government, Universidad de los Andes 3 Faculty of Law, Universidad de los Andes October 2, 2026 Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support legal practice, education, and research, yet their reliability in national legal systems outside the United States remains largely undocumented. We introduce an expert-validated benchmark for evaluating LLM reliability on the Colombian legal system. The benchmark comprises 1042 1042 items spanning ten areas of law and three question formats—closed single-best-answer multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended (IRAC)—built through a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review. We evaluate 15 15 contemporary proprietary and open-weight models, scoring each question format with format-appropriate metrics. Accuracy on closed questions ranges widely, from 0.905 0.905 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to 0.577 0.577 ; but on free-text legal answers, factual correctness never exceeds 0.45 0.45 for any model. Both metrics range from 0 0 to 1 1 , where 1 1 denotes a perfect score. We find a dissociation between answer relevancy and correctness (Spearman ρ = − 0.46 \rho=-0.46 ), so that models reliably sound responsive while frequently being wrong , a pattern of particular concern for non-expert users. Closed-question accuracy and free-text correctness are strongly rank-correlated ( ρ = 0.94 \rho=0.94 ), so cheap multiple-choice screening predicts model ranking but overstates absolute reliability. The free-text ranking proves robust, because an independent rubric-based LLM judge and blind human expert scoring both reproduce it ( ρ ≥ 0.88 \rho\geq 0.88 ). That judge, validated against the human experts, further reveals that the norms models cite are frequently unreliable—only about half are correct, and the rest cite the wrong norm or one that does not exist. Reliability varies systematically by legal area and follows an inverted-U across question complexity. Our results indicate that current LLMs require expert supervision for Colombian legal tasks, and that grounding answers in authoritative sources is a promising path to higher reliability. We release the benchmark construction pipeline to support reproducible evaluation. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have moved quickly from novelty to a working tool in the legal profession. A 2023 UNESCO global survey found that 40 40 % of surveyed judges, lawyers, and other judicial operators had already used ChatGPT or similar tools for work, most often to search for legal information (case law, statutes, doctrine) and to draft documents [ 11 ] . No comparable survey exists for Colombia, but the Consejo Superior de la Judicatura 1 1 1 The Consejo Superior de la Judicatura is the body in charge of administering the Colombian judicial branch. found that roughly one in three of the 3152 3152 judicial employees it surveyed had used AI systems, ChatGPT being the most common [ 3 ] . Adoption, in short, is already widespread and largely unsupervised. These tools, however, exhibit a well-documented failure mode. LLMs hallucinate , producing fluent but incorrect or fabricated legal content [ 4 ] . Lawyers and judges in several countries have pasted tool-generated text—including citations to non-existent statutes and case law—into briefs and judicial decisions without verification [ 10 , 12 ] . Empirical studies in the United States quantify the risk. General-purpose models such as GPT-4 hallucinate on more than half of legal queries and struggle to recognize their own errors [ 4 ] , and even commercial tools marketed as “hallucination-free,” such as Lexis+ AI and Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, answer incorrectly between 17 17 % and 33 33 % of the time despite using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [ 14 ] . Almost all of this evidence concerns English-language, U.S. common law. Empirical research on LLM reliability in Spanish-speaking, civil-law jurisdictions—and on Colombian law in particular—remains scarce; a recent systematic review finds no dedicated Spanish-language legal QA benchmark for Latin America [ 15 ] . The gap matters because linguistic, terminological, and normative differences mean that findings obtained in English do not transfer automatically to Spanish legal practice, and commercial AI systems are not typically representative of Latin American legal diversity. The one prior assessment for Colombia concluded that, as of 2024, no evaluated model reached an accuracy acceptable for practical legal use [ 1 ] , but it predates the current generation of frontier models and covered a very limited set of areas and question types. We address this gap with a systematic, expert-validated evaluation of LLM reliability on the Colombian legal system. Our contributions are: • An expert-validated Colombian legal benchmark of 1042 1042 items spanning ten areas of law and three question formats—closed single-best-answer multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended (IRAC)—built through a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review (Sections 3 – 4 ). • A reproducible evaluation of 15 15 contemporary LLMs , proprietary and open-weight, scored with format-appropriate metrics computed over explicit question subsets (Section 5 ). • An analysis of where and how models fail (Section 6 ), including a dissociation between answer relevancy and correctness—models reliably sound responsive while frequently being wrong —and a characterization of reliability by legal area and question complexity. 2 Related Work 2.1 Legal hallucinations and the reliability of LLMs A growing body of literature measures how often LLMs produce incorrect legal content. Dahl et al. [4] provide the first systematic profile of legal hallucinations in public-facing models, reporting hallucination rates above 50 50 % on a range of tasks and a typology of failure modes. Magesh et al. [14] extend this to commercial, RAG-based legal research tools, showing that “hallucination-free” claims are overstated and that error rates of 17 17 – 33 33 % persist. Complementarily, Guha et al. [8] introduce LegalBench, a collaboratively built benchmark for legal reasoning, establishing the value of task-structured, expert-informed evaluation. For open-ended legal answers, where correctness is not a single string, Salinas et al. [18] conduct a blinded study in which sixteen U.S. law professors rate LLM and peer short answers; the models are preferred over human peers, and the authors show that a separate LLM acting as a judge reproduces expert agreement, supporting LLM-as-a-judge as a scalable, expert-aligned evaluation method for judgment-rich legal tasks. Our work adopts this evaluation philosophy—and a reference-anchored LLM-judge protocol in the same spirit—but targets a non-U.S., civil-law jurisdiction and explicitly separates recognition (closed questions) from generation (free text). 2.2 AI in the Justice System in Latin America and Colombia A parallel literature documents the adoption and governance of AI in judicial and public-sector settings. Global and regional surveys map where and how judicial operators use these tools [ 11 , 3 , 6 ] , and guidance has begun to emerge on their responsible use in courts [ 12 , 9 ] . In Colombia specifically, studies have examined automated decision-making in the public sector [ 13 , 7 ] , the use of AI in the Attorney General’s Office [ 16 ] , and the Constitutional Court’s PretorIA system for processing human-rights cases [ 17 ] . Critical appraisals caution against uncritical reliance on LLMs in judicial decision-making [ 10 , 2 ] . [15] . In these tasks, later commands often depend on information or intermediate results produced by earlier commands. However, existing trajectory-level and step-level credit assignment methods do not explicitly trace the read-write dependencies through which commands affect the final outcome. Consequently, training signals could still be assigned to irrelevant operations, weakening learning from relevant steps.
